item.title: CPV Codes UK: 5 Steps to Pick Codes and Set Alerts 2026
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: CPV codes UK guide for SMEs: how the 8-digit code works, how to shortlist 3-5 codes, and how to set email alerts on Find a Tender and Contracts Finder.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

In the UK, CPV codes (Common Procurement Vocabulary) are the standard numbers public buyers use to label what a contract is for. That makes them the most reliable way for a supplier to filter tenders. The fastest way to use them: find your codes with the Industry CPV code filter on Find a Tender, shortlist 3-5 that match your work, then save the search with email alerts so new notices come to you. Do the same on Contracts Finder to catch notices for procurements that started under the older rules. Both services are free. The government's Central Digital Platform factsheet says "you should not pay to view opportunities in the public sector."

Which option is right for you?

Most small suppliers should begin with Find a Tender, because since 24 February 2025 it is where new procurements under the Procurement Act 2023 are published (GOV.UK factsheet). Pick your starting point from the table.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner who has never searched for tendersOne Find a Tender search: your main keyword plus 1-2 CPV codes, no other filtersFind a Tender search
You bid regularly and want new opportunities every daySaved searches with email alerts on Find a Tender, plus a backup saved search on Contracts FinderFind a Tender sign-in, then Save search
Zero budgetThe free government portals only; avoid paid alert services until you know your codesFind a Tender
Charity, CIC or social enterpriseFind a Tender with Suitability set to VCSE, plus light-touch service codes (see below)Procurement Regulations 2024, Schedule 1
You sell into Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland as wellAdd the devolved portals (Public Contracts Scotland, Sell2Wales, eTendersNI) or a paid aggregatorSee "Next steps"

Why it works this way: Find a Tender is the legal home for new notices. Contracts Finder remains in place for contracts let under PCR 2015, so it still matters but shrinks over time. Our Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender comparison covers the split in more depth.

What Is a CPV Code in the UK?

A CPV code is a standard number that classifies what a public contract buys: goods, works or services. UK buyers attach CPV codes to their tender notices, and suppliers search and filter on them.

The system started in the EU. It was introduced by Regulation (EC) No 2195/2002 and last substantially revised by Regulation (EC) No 213/2008. The UK kept it after Brexit as retained law and still amends it: the Common Procurement Vocabulary (Amendment) Regulations 2023, in force from 29 June 2023, changed the wording of codes 85311200-4 and 85312120-6 from "handicapped" to "disabled people" and "disabled". In other words, the UK now maintains its own copy of the list in UK law.

The codes also have legal effect under the Procurement Act 2023. The Procurement Regulations 2024, Schedule 1 defines "light touch" services, such as health, social care, education and some legal services, by listing CPV codes. Services marked "R" in that table can be reserved for public service mutuals. If you are a charity or social enterprise delivering care or community services, the CPV code on a notice can tell you which rules that procurement follows.

Some figures on the size of the list (as of October 2026): the main vocabulary has about 9,454 codes, according to the European Commission's CPV 2008 guide. The independent lookup site cpvcodes.eu counts those codes across 45 divisions, plus 903 supplementary codes.

For example, a notice for office cleaning at a council depot would usually carry a code from the 9091 cleaning-services family. A cleaning company that filters on that family will see it even if the title just says "Depot Facilities Services Lot 2".

What Are CPV Codes Made Of? (Structure Explained)

Each CPV code has 8 digits plus a check digit. The digits run from broad to specific: division, group, class, then category. The EU regulation sets out the pattern:

LevelDigits that matterPatternExample
DivisionFirst 2XX000000-Y90000000 (sewage, refuse, cleaning and environmental services)
GroupFirst 3XXX00000-Y90900000 (cleaning and sanitation services)
ClassFirst 4XXXX0000-Y90910000-9 (cleaning services)
CategoryFirst 5XXXXX000-Y90911000 (accommodation, building and window cleaning)
More specificDigits 6-8XXXXXXXX-Y90911200-8 (building-cleaning services)

The digit after the hyphen is the check digit. It verifies the first eight digits and catches typos (EU regulation), but it doesn't describe anything. When you search, the first eight digits are what count.

Trailing zeros tell you how broad a code is. 45000000-7 (construction work) sits at the top of a whole division. A code with no trailing zeros is a single, narrow item. Here is how to read any code you come across:

  1. Ignore the check digit after the hyphen.
  2. Count the trailing zeros. Six zeros means a division, five a group, four a class, three a category.
  3. Trim the code back one digit at a time to see its parent level, and check the parent covers your work too.
  4. Look at the sibling codes under the same parent. Buyers often choose a neighbour of the code you expected.

There is also a supplementary vocabulary. Its codes are alphanumeric: a letter for the section followed by digits (Wikipedia summary of the CPV regulation). It adds detail such as purpose or material. You will rarely need it to find tenders, because portal filters work on the main 8-digit codes.

Where to Find the Official UK CPV Codes List

The authoritative list is the annex to Regulation (EC) No 213/2008, as amended in UK law by SI 2023/601. For day-to-day use, the best list is the one built into the Industry CPV code filter on Find a Tender and Contracts Finder, because those are the codes buyers actually pick from.

Which source to use for what:

SourceUse it forLimitation
EUR-Lex Regulation 213/2008The legal text and full annexA long PDF that is hard to browse; doesn't include the UK wording changes
legislation.gov.uk SI 2023/601UK amendmentsOnly shows the changes, not the whole list
Find a Tender searchPicking codes and checking live noticesYou need to sign in to save searches
Contracts Finder searchOlder-regime and historic noticesHolds no notices posted before 26 February 2015 (shown on the search page)
Procurement Regulations 2024, Schedule 1Light-touch service codesOnly covers light-touch services
Third-party lookups, e.g. cpvcodes.euQuick keyword browsingNot official; the site says it isn't affiliated with the European Commission

Pitfalls and fixes:

  • Copying a code from a blog list without checking it. Paste the first eight digits into the Find a Tender CPV filter. If it doesn't appear, or the description is different, use the portal's version.
  • Using the EU's newer TED interface as your UK source. TED covers EU tenders. UK notices are on Find a Tender, so build your UK searches there.
  • Treating Contracts Finder as the whole market. Under the Procurement Act, procurements started from 24 February 2025 only need notices on Find a Tender. Treat Find a Tender as your main source.

How to Find CPV Codes on GOV.UK (Find a Tender & Contracts Finder)

Both GOV.UK portals have a filter labelled Industry CPV code, where you pick codes before you run and save a search. The labels below are taken from the live search pages (as of October 2026).

On Find a Tender

  1. Go to find-tender.service.gov.uk/Search/Results.
  2. Type your main trade word, for example "grounds maintenance", into Keywords. This searches titles, descriptions, identifiers and organisation names.
  3. Open Industry CPV code and search or browse for the matching code. Tick it.
  4. Under Procurement stage, choose Open opportunities if you only want things you can bid for now. Add Pipeline or Planning if you want early warning.
  5. Optional: set Contract location to the regions you can serve, and under Suitability tick SME or VCSE.
  6. Sort by Published (newest), then run the search.
  7. Open 5-10 results and check the CPV codes listed on each notice. Add any useful codes you hadn't thought of to your shortlist.

Other filters on the page include Notice type (the Procurement Act notices UK1-UK17 and the older F and T forms), Value, Commercial tool (Framework, Dynamic market, Dynamic purchasing system and others) and Date range. If frameworks or dynamic markets are part of your plan, see our guides on getting onto a framework agreement and dynamic purchasing systems.

On Contracts Finder

  1. Go to contractsfinder.service.gov.uk/Search/Results.
  2. Fill in Keywords, then open Industry CPV code and pick the same codes as on Find a Tender.
  3. Set Procurement stage to Opportunity and Notice status to Open.
  4. If it fits, set Notice suitability to SME or VCSE, and Location of contract to a region or a postcode with a distance.
  5. Click Update results.

For example, a landscaping sole trader in Leicestershire might run "grounds maintenance" with CPV 77314000-4 (grounds maintenance services), Open opportunities, and East Midlands as the location. That is an illustration of the filter combination, not a forecast of how many tenders will show up.

How to Choose the Right CPV Code for Your Business

Begin with the keyword for your main service or product. Test it in the Find a Tender CPV search, then shortlist 3-5 codes (a main code plus related ones) instead of relying on one broad code. These five steps will get you there.

Step 1: Write down what buyers call your work

Buyers use procurement language. A "window cleaner" may be buying "building-cleaning services". A "web agency" may be buying "website design services". List 3-4 phrases that describe how a council or NHS trust would word your service in a specification.

Step 2: Find the code that matches your core work

Search each phrase in Industry CPV code on Find a Tender. Choose the most specific code that still covers your main service. For an office cleaner that might be 90919200-4 (office cleaning services), with 90910000-9 (cleaning services) as the broader parent.

Step 3: Add the parent and 1-3 siblings

Buyers don't always pick the narrowest code, so add the parent class and the neighbouring codes you could deliver. Use the trim-a-digit method from the structure section.

Example shortlists (illustrations; check every code in the portal before relying on it):

BusinessMain codeRelated codes to test
Commercial cleaner90919200-4 Office cleaning90911200-8 Building-cleaning; 90910000-9 Cleaning services
Web design studio72413000-8 Website design72000000-5 IT services (broad, test the volume first)
Training provider80500000-9 Training servicesCodes from division 80 that match your subjects
Catering social enterprise55520000-1 Catering servicesCheck Schedule 1 to see whether it counts as light touch
Community care charity85310000-5 Social work servicesLight-touch codes in Schedule 1

Step 4: Check the shortlist against real notices

Run a search with your shortlisted codes and read the results. A good code returns mostly contracts you could bid for. If more than half the results are irrelevant, the code is too broad. If you see almost nothing over the last few months, add the parent or a sibling. Then check the awarded side too: set Procurement stage to Award or Contract, look at notices won by businesses like yours, and note their codes.

Step 5: Pair each code with a keyword set

Codes catch notices that use unusual wording. Keywords catch notices that a buyer coded badly. Running both, in separate saved searches, gives you the widest safe coverage (next section).

How to Set Up Daily Alerts Using CPV Codes

When your shortlist is ready, save it as a search with email alerts on both Find a Tender and Contracts Finder. New matching notices will then reach you without you having to search each morning. Both services are free (as of October 2026; check the official page).

Find a Tender

  1. Make sure you have a Find a Tender account. The GOV.UK factsheet lists "Set up alerts for tenders of interest" as a supplier feature, and it's the same account you use to register your organisation. Our Find a Tender registration guide walks through it.
  2. Run your search with Industry CPV code, Procurement stage and any location or suitability filters.
  3. Choose Save search and sign in when asked. The search page says a saved search appears "in your list of saved searches, so you can easily run it again", and that you "can choose to receive emails when new notices are published that meet your search criteria."
  4. Switch on the email option and give the search a clear name, such as "CPV 9091 cleaning, open, East Midlands".
  5. Save a second search that uses Keywords only, with no CPV codes, as a safety net.

Contracts Finder

  1. Run the same search and click Update results.
  2. Click Save search. Register or sign in if asked. A GOV.UK Contracts Finder supplier guide says the alerts are free, that you can create as many as you like, and that you name each search and choose whether and how often to get emails. The guide dates from 2011, so the screen labels may have changed.
  3. Manage your alerts later from your profile page.

A 10-minute daily routine

  • Open the alert emails. Discard anything outside your region, value range or capacity straight away.
  • For anything promising, open the notice and check the closing date, the lots and whether there is an SME/VCSE suitability flag.
  • Once a week, run your saved searches by hand sorted by Published (newest) to check the alerts are firing.
  • Once a month, look at which codes produced the useful notices and drop the ones that only bring noise.

Pitfalls: an alert filtered to Open opportunities will never show pipeline or planning notices, which are often your earliest warning. Keep one wider saved search for them. Also, saved searches from accounts on the old Find a Tender service were carried over to the new accounts. If you had an old account, review those searches rather than leaving them running unchecked.

CPV Codes vs UNSPSC and Other Classification Systems

CPV is the system used for UK and EU public contract notices. UNSPSC is a separate global classification that some organisations use for their internal catalogues and spending data. For finding UK tenders, CPV is the one that counts.

SystemWho uses itWhere you'll see itShould an SME searching for UK tenders use it?
CPVUK and EU public buyersEvery Find a Tender and Contracts Finder notice (used by UK buyers per Tussell)Yes, it is the main filter
UNSPSCPrivate and public sector, internationallySome buyer catalogues; NHS product classificationOnly if a buyer's catalogue or e-procurement system asks for it
GS1 (GTIN, GPC)Product supply chains, incl. NHSNHS product identificationOnly if you supply physical products to the NHS
eCl@ssMainly industrial companiesEngineering and manufacturing cataloguesRarely relevant to UK public tenders
SIC codesCompanies HouseYour company registrationNo, a SIC code is not a CPV code

The usual mix-up is with SIC codes. Your Companies House SIC code describes your company, while a CPV code describes a contract. You won't find tenders by typing your SIC code into the CPV filter. A supplier selling medical consumables to NHS trusts may need CPV codes to find tenders and also UNSPSC or GS1 codes once they are listed in a catalogue. Those are separate steps that happen at different stages.

Common Mistakes When Using CPV Codes to Search for Contracts

The most common mistakes are using one code that is too broad or too narrow, ignoring related secondary codes, and never updating saved searches. Each one has a simple fix.

Only using a top-level division code. If you filter on 45000000-7 (construction work), most results will be jobs you can't bid for. Fix: move down to the class or category that matches your trade, and keep the division only for an occasional manual scan.

Only using one very narrow code. A buyer may file your kind of work under the parent or a sibling code. Fix: add the parent and 1-3 siblings (Step 3 above).

Ignoring secondary codes on notices. Multi-service contracts often carry several codes. The main code might be facilities management while your cleaning work sits in a secondary code or a single lot. Fix: when you read notices, record every code listed, not just the first one.

Relying on codes alone. Buyers sometimes miscode notices. Fix: keep a keyword-only saved search running alongside your CPV search.

Filtering out SME-suitable work by accident. The Suitability box is useful, but not every buyer ticks it. Fix: run one version with it and one without, then compare.

Never revisiting searches. Your services change, and so does buyer behaviour. Fix: review your codes each quarter using the notices you actually bid on.

Missing how light-touch codes affect the rules. For care, education and community services, the code can put a procurement under the light-touch regime (Schedule 1), which allows more flexible procedures and sometimes reserved contracts. Fix: check Schedule 1 for your codes before you plan a bid.

Finding the notice is only the start. After that you will face the selection questionnaire and the scoring, which our guide on how to win government contracts covers.

Next steps

You can have a working CPV setup today using only the free GOV.UK portals.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open Find a Tender, test your main keyword in Industry CPV code, and write down a shortlist of 3-5 codes.
  2. Save two searches with email alerts: one based on CPV codes and one keyword-only safety net. Then repeat the CPV search on Contracts Finder and click Save search.
  3. Put a monthly reminder in your calendar to check which codes brought you useful notices and to cut the rest.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: paid alert services combine the UK portals into one feed. For example, PSIP monitors Find a Tender, Contracts Finder, Public Contracts Scotland, Sell2Wales and eTendersNI. Its Essential plan costs £199 a month plus VAT for a daily digest and 6 saved alerts. Growth costs £599 a month for alerts every 4 hours, and there is a 14-day free trial (as of October 2026; check the official page). It suits businesses that bid across several UK nations and want one inbox. It is not for a sole trader serving one English region: the free Find a Tender alerts cover the same English notices, and £199 a month is a big cost before you have won anything. A paid service still uses the codes you give it, so you need to choose the right codes either way.

FAQ

What are CPV codes used for?

Buyers use CPV codes to classify the subject of a public contract in a standard way. Suppliers use them to filter and get alerts for relevant notices. In UK law they also define which services count as light touch under the Procurement Regulations 2024.

Are CPV codes still used in the UK after Brexit?

Yes. The UK kept the CPV regulation and has amended it itself, for example through SI 2023/601 in June 2023. Both Find a Tender and Contracts Finder have an Industry CPV code search filter.

How many digits does a CPV code have?

A CPV code has eight digits plus a check digit after a hyphen, for example 45000000-7. The first two digits give the division, and each further digit narrows it down (Regulation 213/2008). The check digit only guards against typing errors.

Can I search Contracts Finder by CPV code only?

Yes. Leave Keywords empty, choose codes under Industry CPV code, and click Update results. A codes-only search misses notices that buyers coded badly, though, so keep a keyword search running too. Also search Find a Tender, because new Procurement Act notices don't have to appear on Contracts Finder.

item.title: Dynamic Purchasing System: 6 SME Steps for 2026
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Dynamic purchasing system rules changed: how UK SMEs join a dynamic market or legacy DPS, stay a member and bid, with 2026 thresholds and 2029 cut-off.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

A dynamic purchasing system (DPS) is an open list of qualified suppliers that a public buyer sets up so it can run quick mini-competitions for individual contracts. Unlike a framework, suppliers can apply to join at any point while it runs. Under the Procurement Act 2023 the new version is called a dynamic market. Older DPSs set up under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 can still run, but they must end by 23 February 2029 at the latest. For an SME the process is short: find the notice, register, pass the membership conditions, stay eligible, then bid on each call-off you can win.

Which option is right for you?

Your first step depends on whether you're new to public tendering, already on a legacy DPS, or working with very little time or budget.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never bid for public workRegister on Find a Tender and join one dynamic market in your core tradeFind a Tender supplier registration guide
You missed a framework windowA dynamic market in the same category, because joining stays open throughout its termFind a Tender search
Already on a legacy (PCR 2015) DPSNote the end date and watch for its replacement dynamic marketThe DPS notice on Find a Tender or Contracts Finder
Daily bidding, several tradesApply for several lots or categories in one market, but only ones you can deliverThe market's eSourcing portal (for example Delta eSourcing)
Tight budget, small jobs under £30kContracts Finder and quotes, not a dynamic market/contracts-finder-vs-find-a-tender-2026-table-and-steps/
Utilities supplier (water, energy, transport)Check for qualifying utilities dynamic markets, where tender notices can go only to membersFind a Tender notice types

Why these picks: if you're a beginner, one market in your strongest trade keeps the admin manageable. If you missed a framework, a dynamic market is the main route back in before the framework is re-let. If you're on a legacy DPS, the 2029 deadline means your membership can't continue in its current form.

What Is a Dynamic Purchasing System (DPS)?

A DPS is an open, list-based procurement tool. Qualified suppliers can join at any time and then bid for individual call-off contracts as the buyer advertises them. The government's dynamic markets guidance describes a dynamic market as "a list of qualified suppliers" who are eligible for future procurements. It says the dynamic market replaces both the DPS and the utilities "qualification system", and that it must stay open to new suppliers at any time.

Most people still say "DPS", so here's how the two names relate:

  • Legacy DPS: set up under regulation 34 of the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR 2015). It keeps running under the old rules, but its period of validity could not be changed after 23 February 2026, and it expires at the end of 23 February 2029 if it hasn't already ended.
  • Dynamic market: set up under sections 34–40 of the Procurement Act 2023, which has applied to new procurements since 24 February 2025. Under the old rules a DPS was meant for "commonly used" purchases. That restriction has gone, according to Osborne Clarke's analysis.

For example, a real legacy DPS is the former Crown Commercial Service RM6124 Communications Marketplace. It was extended for 17 months to 23/02/29, which uses the full transitional allowance. Crown Commercial Service itself became the Government Commercial Agency (GCA) on 1 April 2026, so you'll now find its agreements on gca.gov.uk.

How Do Dynamic Purchasing Systems Work?

The buyer opens a list by category. Suppliers apply and are admitted if they meet the conditions. After that, only members compete for each contract the buyer advertises through the market.

Under the Procurement Act 2023, a dynamic market follows this sequence:

  1. Intention notice (UK13). The buyer publishes a dynamic market intention notice "to notify suppliers that they can apply to join."
  2. Membership applications. The buyer must accept applications at any time during the market's term and consider them within a reasonable period. It must admit every supplier that meets the conditions and isn't excluded or excludable (s.36). The buyer can't cap the number of members.
  3. Establishment notice (UK14). This is published once the market is set up. It tells other contracting authorities they can use it and shows which suppliers are members.
  4. Modification notices (UK15). Each time suppliers are added or removed, the buyer publishes a dynamic market modification notice. Busy markets publish these often.
  5. Call-off competitions. For each contract, the buyer runs the competitive flexible procedure, and that is the only procedure allowed (guidance, para 10). It usually publishes a UK4 tender notice. Tenders from non-members must be disregarded (s.34).
  6. Cessation notice (UK16). This is published when the market stops operating.

For example, Oak National Academy's "Digital Product Development and Support Services" dynamic market shows the whole lifecycle on its Find a Tender record. It had an intention notice in September 2025, was established in November 2025, had several modification notices, and a cessation notice followed on 20 October 2026.

On fees: in a non-utilities dynamic market, the buyer can only charge fees to suppliers that win a contract, and only as a fixed percentage of that contract's estimated value (s.38). Utilities dynamic markets can charge membership fees as well. Look for the percentage in the tender documents before you price.

How to Set Up a Dynamic Purchasing System (Buyer Side, Briefly)

A contracting authority sets up a dynamic market by publishing notices on Find a Tender and setting proportionate membership conditions. It then keeps the market open for its whole term. This section is short because the rest of this guide is about the supplier side. Knowing the buyer's rules still helps, because it tells you what you're entitled to.

The buyer's main obligations are:

  1. Publish a UK13 intention notice before the market is established (s.39).
  2. Set conditions for membership that only check legal and financial capacity and technical ability. Section 36 stops buyers requiring audited accounts unless the law already requires the supplier to have them. It also bans insurance requirements before award and any requirement to have held a particular previous contract.
  3. Fix the conditions for the market's life. Conditions "cannot be modified during the life of the dynamic market" (guidance, para 23).
  4. Publish UK14, UK15 and UK16 notices at establishment, each modification and cessation.
  5. Choose a duration. The Act sets no maximum term for a dynamic market. Legacy DPSs, by contrast, are capped at 23 February 2029.

Points 2 and 3 matter most to SMEs. If a membership questionnaire asks for three years of audited accounts from a micro-business that isn't legally required to have them, you can raise it with the buyer and cite section 36.

How to Join and Stay Qualified in an Open DPS (SME Steps)

You can apply whenever the notice is live. Once you pass the membership conditions you're in, and you stay in as long as you keep meeting them and don't become an excluded supplier. These six steps cover both new dynamic markets and legacy DPSs.

Step 1: Find the right market

Open Find a Tender and search for "dynamic market" plus your trade (for example, "dynamic market grounds maintenance"). Legacy DPSs often show up under "dynamic purchasing system" on both Find a Tender and Contracts Finder. If you're not sure which service lists what, see /contracts-finder-vs-find-a-tender-2026-table-and-steps/.

Before you apply, check three things on the notice: the end date, the lots or categories, and the portal link. A market that has a UK16 cessation notice is closed, even if the old pages still come up in search.

Step 2: Register on the Central Digital Platform

Under the Act, buyers expect your core supplier information to come from Find a Tender. The government's three-step guide uses these labels:

  1. Create a GOV.UK One Login, then choose Register an organisation and select Supplier. Have your Companies House number (or equivalent) and registered address ready.
  2. Open your organisation and select Complete supplier information. Fill in basic information, connected persons, qualifications, trade assurances, exclusions and financial information.
  3. Select Share my information, confirm the declaration, then select Confirm and get share code.

Registration is free. Charities and sole traders without a Companies House number can register using an equivalent identifier.

Step 3: Register on the buyer's eSourcing portal

Most markets take applications through a separate portal. For example, Embark Multi Academy Trust's "Estates Works and Capital Projects Dynamic Market" takes applications through Delta eSourcing. You paste your share code into the portal or upload the supplier information file, whichever the buyer asks for.

Step 4: Answer the membership conditions

This works like a selection questionnaire: the buyer checks capacity and ability, not price or quality. Answer only the categories you can actually deliver. The Embark market says suppliers can apply for one or more categories and aren't required to provide every service within a category. For how to answer capability and exclusion questions, see /selection-questionnaire-procurement-act-2023-7-sme-steps/.

Step 5: Confirm admission

The Act requires the buyer to consider your application "within a reasonable period" (s.36). It doesn't set a fixed number of days, so read the buyer's documents for its own target. If you're admitted, your name should appear in the next UK15 modification notice. If you're rejected, ask which condition you failed. You can reapply at any time once you've fixed the gap.

Step 6: Stay qualified

There's no statutory annual renewal for dynamic market members. Removal happens when your circumstances change:

  • The buyer must remove you if you become an excluded supplier, for example by being added to the debarment list. It may remove you if you stop meeting the membership conditions, or if you became excludable after joining or already were when admitted (s.37 and guidance paras 24–26). The buyer has to tell you the reasons.
  • If your details change (new director, new address, lapsed accreditation), update Complete supplier information and generate a new share code. The registration guide says changes need a new code and file.
  • Legacy DPS terms often add their own re-verification checks, such as yearly insurance or accreditation evidence. These come from the contract, not the Act, so read your DPS terms for any deadlines.

Common mistakes and fixes

MistakeWhat happensFix
Applying to every lotYou get invitations you can't price, and declining a lot looks badApply only to lots you could start next month
Old share code in the portalThe buyer sees outdated directors or financialsGenerate a new code after every change
Ignoring a legacy DPS end dateMembership disappears on or before 23 Feb 2029Note the date and watch for a UK13 notice for the replacement
Treating admission as a winAdmission guarantees no workBudget time for each call-off tender (see below)
Missing call-off invitationsInvites often go only to the portal inboxAdd the portal's notification address to your safe senders

Bidding inside the market

Every call-off is a full competition among members, judged on the award criteria in that tender. Above threshold, the normal minimum tendering period for a UK4 notice is 25 days when electronic submission is allowed and all documents are published with the notice. Buyers often score social value too, so keep reusable evidence ready (see /social-value-in-tenders-ppn-002-steps-and-answer-examples/).

Threshold specifics

From 1 January 2026, the Act's thresholds (including VAT) are £135,018 for central government goods and services, £207,720 for sub-central bodies such as councils and NHS trusts, £5,193,000 for works and £663,540 for light-touch services (as of October 2026; check the official notice).

This matters for dynamic markets. The government's guidance says setting membership conditions is a suitability assessment, and section 85(1) prohibits that for regulated below-threshold contracts. So a dynamic market can't be used to award below-threshold contracts. If your typical job is a £40,000 council repair, it will probably come through an open tender or a quote, not a dynamic market.

Dynamic Purchasing System vs Framework Agreement

The main difference is entry. A framework fixes its supplier list when it's awarded, while a DPS or dynamic market stays open to new suppliers for its whole term. That's why a dynamic market matters if you missed a framework deadline.

FeatureFramework (Procurement Act 2023)Dynamic market / DPS
When you can joinOnly at award; open frameworks reopen at set pointsAny time during the term (s.36)
Supplier capBuyer can limit numbersNo limit allowed
What gets assessed to joinA full tender, usually including price and qualityCapacity and ability conditions only
Maximum termNormally 4 years (s.47); open framework scheme up to 8 years (s.49)No statutory maximum; legacy DPS ends by 23 Feb 2029
Call-off methodDirect award or competition, as set in the frameworkCompetitive flexible procedure only
Fees to suppliersSet by framework termsNon-utilities: only a fixed % on contracts won (s.38)
Below-threshold usePossible, under the Act's below-threshold rulesNot permitted

Open frameworks sit in between. They must be reopened at least once in the first three years and then at least every five years, and the scheme ends after eight years at most (s.49). Between reopenings, though, they're still closed.

For example, a cleaning firm that missed a council's facilities framework would otherwise wait up to four years for the re-let. If the same council runs a cleaning dynamic market, the firm could apply this week. Framework call-offs can also be awarded directly without a competition, which can't happen inside a dynamic market. For the framework route, see /framework-agreement-how-to-get-on-6-sme-steps-2026/.

Dynamic Purchasing System Examples

Live UK examples range from school estates works to digital services and marketing. You can check any of them on Find a Tender or the GCA site.

ExampleBuyerTypeDetail (source)
Estates Works and Capital Projects Dynamic MarketEmbark Multi Academy TrustDynamic market (Act)Established 26 March 2026; 47+ trade categories including roofing, HVAC, electrical and asbestos removal; open to other contracting authorities; applications via Delta eSourcing (FTS)
Digital Product Development and Support ServicesOak National AcademyDynamic market (Act)Established November 2025; Lot 1 web development; cessation notice 20 October 2026 (FTS)
RM6124 Communications MarketplaceFormer CCS, now GCALegacy DPSExtended 17 months to 23/02/29 (Contracts Finder)
RM6126 Research & InsightsFormer CCS, now GCALegacy DPSListed as expiring 23/02/2029 (GCA agreement page)
OneLondon Local Health and Care Record Exemplar DPSNHS / London health partnersLegacy DPSHealth data and digital services (FTS)

The Embark example is a useful model for trades businesses. One academy trust set up the market, four other trusts were named as early adopters, and other contracting authorities can use it. Joining once can therefore get you invited to call-offs from several buyers.

The Oak example is a warning: a dynamic market can close well before you expect it to. Check for a UK16 notice before you spend time on an application.

Dynamic Purchasing System Pros and Cons

For SMEs, the main advantage is that you can join at any time and the entry test is light. The cost is ongoing admin and a fresh competition for every contract.

ProsCons
Join at any time, so missing a deadline isn't fatalAdmission wins nothing; every call-off is a new tender
Conditions limited to capacity and ability, with no audited accounts unless legally required (s.36)No cap on members, so a popular lot can attract many bidders
No upfront fee in non-utilities markets; fees only on contracts wonA fee percentage on won work cuts your margin
One membership can serve several buyersInvitations arrive at short notice and need quick turnaround
Fixed conditions, so the rules don't change mid-termLegacy DPS memberships end by 23 Feb 2029
Removal must come with reasonsCan't be used for below-threshold work, which is where many micro-businesses bid

Pitfall and fix: the biggest risk is staying a passive member. If invitations arrive and you never bid, nothing happens. Set yourself a rule, such as reviewing every invitation within two working days and either bidding or declining. Pick the lots where your price and delivery record are strongest.

What Is a Pseudo Dynamic Purchasing System?

"Pseudo-DPS" is informal shorthand, not a legal term in the Procurement Act 2023 or PCR 2015. It describes an arrangement that works like a DPS but isn't set up under the formal DPS or dynamic market rules. The Act's definitions cover frameworks, open frameworks and dynamic markets, and Find a Tender's notice types have no "pseudo" category.

In practice the label has been used for approved supplier lists, often for lower-value work, and for framework-style arrangements that let new suppliers in from time to time. Under PCR 2015, a real DPS could be used for below-threshold contracts, so the line between them was blurred. Under the Act that changes: suitability-based membership is banned for regulated below-threshold contracts (section 85(1)). An approved list that checks suppliers before letting them quote for those contracts is on shaky legal ground.

For example, if a council emails you about joining its "pseudo-DPS for minor works", check what sits behind it:

  1. Search Find a Tender for the buyer's name and look for a UK13 or UK14 notice (a dynamic market), a UK4 notice that establishes a framework or open framework, or an old DPS notice.
  2. If none exists, treat it as an informal list. It won't give you the statutory rights covered above, such as acceptance at any time and written reasons for removal.
  3. Ask the buyer in writing which procedure it was set up under.

Go by the notice type, not by what the buyer calls the arrangement.

Next steps

Pick one market, get registered and apply before the end of the week.

Today, on your own:

  1. Search Find a Tender for "dynamic market" plus your trade, and list up to three live markets with their end dates. Skip any with a UK16 notice.
  2. Create your GOV.UK One Login and complete Complete supplier information to get a share code (guide).
  3. If you're already on a legacy DPS, put 23 February 2029 in your calendar along with the DPS's own end date, if that comes sooner.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: you can hire a freelance bid writer or a tender consultancy to handle registration, membership answers and call-off bids. There's no official price list. Fees depend on the provider and scope, so ask for a fixed written quote per application or per bid (as of October 2026; check each provider's own terms). This suits businesses that expect regular call-off invitations but have no one in-house to write bids. It's a poor fit if you're testing one small market, because joining is mostly factual data entry you can do for free. Its main limitation is that a consultant can't create delivery evidence or accreditations you don't have, and you remain responsible for the declarations you submit. Find a Tender registration and applying to a dynamic market cost nothing.

FAQ

What does dynamic purchasing system mean?

It means a buyer keeps an open list of qualified suppliers that anyone can apply to join during its term, then runs a separate competition among members for each contract. Under the Procurement Act 2023 the same idea is called a dynamic market. Legacy DPSs under PCR 2015 can continue until 23 February 2029 at the latest.

What is a dynamic purchasing system in procurement?

It's a way to award public contracts that sits between a single open tender and a closed framework. Suppliers are checked once for capacity and ability, then compete for each call-off using the competitive flexible procedure. Only members can win, and tenders from non-members must be disregarded (s.34).

How to set up a dynamic purchasing system?

Only a contracting authority can set one up. It publishes a UK13 intention notice on Find a Tender, sets proportionate membership conditions under section 36, and publishes UK14, UK15 and UK16 notices at establishment, modification and closure. New DPSs under the old 2015 rules can't be created for new procurements, so new arrangements are dynamic markets.

What are some dynamic purchasing system examples?

Recent examples include Embark Multi Academy Trust's Estates Works and Capital Projects Dynamic Market (established March 2026, 47+ trade categories). Oak National Academy's digital services dynamic market is another; it ceased in October 2026. Legacy examples include the former CCS RM6124 Communications Marketplace, extended to 23 February 2029.

item.title: Find a Tender Registration: 5 Steps for UK Suppliers 2026
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Find a Tender registration for UK suppliers in 5 steps: GOV.UK One Login, organisation details, PPON, and how it differs from a Companies House number.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

Find a Tender registration is free. You create a GOV.UK One Login, register your business as a Supplier, fill in the Supplier Information sections, and then generate a share code that you give to buyers when you bid (GOV.UK three-step guide). Your "registration number" is the Public Procurement Organisation Number (PPON). The platform issues it when you register your organisation. It is a different thing from your Companies House number, though the Companies House number is often what you use to set up the account. You don't need an account to browse notices. You only need one when you are ready to bid (Central Digital Platform factsheet).

Which option is right for you?

The right first step depends on how close you are to bidding. If you are only exploring, start by searching. If a deadline is coming up, do the full registration now.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, just looking at what's out thereSearch notices without an account. You can register laterFind a Tender search
You've found a tender and want to bidFull supplier registration, then get a share codeGOV.UK: register in three easy steps
You bid regularly as part of daily workRegister, then use saved searches and email notifications on FTSFind a Tender home, "Sign in"
Sole trader or charity with no Companies House numberAnswer "No" to the Companies House question and use your charity number, or let the platform assign an identifierSupplier registration short guide (PDF)
Zero budgetUse the official route. Registering and viewing notices are both freeCDP factsheet

Why each pick makes sense:

  • Beginner: the factsheet says suppliers "only need to register at the point that they want to bid for a contract", so you lose nothing by searching first.
  • Ready to bid: buyers ask for your share code or supplier information file, and you can't get either until registration is finished.
  • Daily use: once you have an account, FTS lets you "save search criteria" and "sign up for notifications via email" (Find a Tender).
  • No Companies House number: the official guide accepts Charity Commission and Scottish Charity Regulator numbers. If you have neither, the platform "will assign you one".
  • Budget: "Find a Tender is free to use for everyone. There are no charges and you should not pay to view opportunities" (factsheet).

What Is Find a Tender (And Who Must Use It)?

Find a Tender Service (FTS) is the UK government's official platform for public procurement notices, run by the Cabinet Office. Since 24 February 2025 it has also been the Central Digital Platform where suppliers register under the Procurement Act 2023 (CDP factsheet).

Find a Tender started out after Brexit as the UK's replacement for publishing high-value notices in the EU's Official Journal. The Procurement Act 2023 widened its role. GOV.UK calls the enhanced service "a fully integrated digital platform where noticing, sign-in and registration, supplier information all work together" (factsheet). On the Find a Tender homepage you can open Notice Search, Opportunities ("Upcoming pipelines and active tenders"), Contracts, Commercial tools (frameworks, dynamic markets and dynamic purchasing systems) and a Payments transparency register.

Who must use it:

  • Buyers (contracting authorities) in England, Wales and Northern Ireland publish their Procurement Act notices here. Procurements started from 24 February 2025 publish both above- and below-threshold notices on Find a Tender. Below-threshold notices in Scotland are the exception (Find a Tender).
  • Suppliers who want to bid for contracts covered by the Act need to be registered and hold a PPON. In practice, buyers ask for your share code or supplier information during the tender.

The thresholds that decide which rules apply

The threshold amounts below apply to procurements that start on or after 1 January 2026. They were set by the Procurement Act 2023 (Threshold Amounts) (Amendment) Regulations 2025 and confirmed in PPN 023. The GOV.UK thresholds guidance confirms the figures include VAT.

Contract type (as of October 2026)Threshold incl. VAT
Central government goods/services£135,018
Sub-central (councils, many NHS bodies) goods/services£207,720
Works£5,193,000
Light touch services (other)£663,540
Utilities (other)£415,440

A common mistake is assuming that Find a Tender only lists very large contracts. Under the Act, below-threshold notices for new procurements go to Find a Tender as well. That means small contracts you could realistically win can turn up there too. Use the Suitability filter for SMEs or VCSEs, covered further down.

How to Sign Up for Find a Tender (Supplier Registration)

You sign up on the Find a Tender website itself. The person setting up the account uses a GOV.UK One Login with a work email address. It costs nothing, and the process is the same for limited companies, sole traders and charities (GOV.UK guide).

Have these ready before you start. They come from the official Supplier Registration short guide and the GOV.UK guidance:

  • A work email address for the person who will be the Administrator
  • A mobile phone or an authenticator app for security codes
  • Your Companies House number, Charity Commission number or Scottish Charity Regulator number, if you have one
  • Your organisation's registered name and registered address
  • A shared organisation email address, for example tenders@yourbusiness.co.uk (this is an example)
  • Your VAT number if you have one, and whether you are an SME, VCSE or public mutual

Decide who the Administrator will be first. The official guide says "Every supplier should assign a single person to initially set up and register their organisation. This person will be the Administrator and will be able to add and approve other users." For a sole trader, that's you. For a charity, choose someone who will still be around when the next tender comes in, not a volunteer on a short placement.

Common sign-up mistakes and fixes

  • Using the wrong website. The Cabinet Office's Supplier Registration Service is "not the same website" as the Central Digital Platform (Supplier Registration Service FAQ). Fix: begin at find-tender.service.gov.uk and select Sign in.
  • Re-registering with a new email address. If you had an older FTS account and come back with a different email, "your old information will not be pulled through" (GOV.UK guide). Fix: use the same email so you keep your saved searches and notices.
  • Paying a third party to "register" you. Registration and viewing opportunities are free (factsheet).

Find a Tender Service Supplier Registration: Step-by-Step Walkthrough

Supplier registration takes five steps. You create a One Login, finish the platform registration, register your organisation, complete Supplier Information, and then share it to get a share code. The labels below are taken from the GOV.UK walkthrough.

Step 1: Create your GOV.UK One Login

  1. Go to Find a Tender and select Sign in.
  2. Select Create your GOV.UK One Login.
  3. Enter your individual work email address, then agree to the terms of use and privacy policy.
  4. Enter the 6-digit security code sent to your email.
  5. Choose a password.
  6. Choose how you want to receive security codes (text message or authenticator app), then enter the code.

Step 2: Complete Central Digital Platform registration

  1. Read and agree to the Central Digital Platform service privacy policy.
  2. Enter your first and last name.
  3. Select Continue.

Step 3: Register your organisation

  1. On your account page, select Register an organisation.
  2. Choose Supplier, not Buyer.
  3. Answer "Do you have a Companies House number?"
  4. Yes: enter the number.
  5. No: you'll see other options, such as a Charity Commission number. If none of them apply, the platform generates a unique identifier for you.
  6. Check or enter your organisation's registered name.
  7. Enter your shared organisation email address.
  8. Check or enter your registered address. Non-UK addresses are accepted.
  9. Review your answers and select Save.

After you save, your organisation has its unique identifier, the PPON (short guide).

Step 4: Complete Supplier Information

Select Complete Supplier Information and work through the six sections listed in the GOV.UK guide:

  • Basic Information
  • Connected Persons
  • Qualifications
  • Trade Assurances
  • Exclusions
  • Financial Information

Most of the effort goes into Connected Persons and Exclusions, because you need accurate details about the people who control the organisation and honest answers to the exclusion questions. You enter this once and reuse it. The factsheet says you can "review it and re-use it every time for each tender".

Step 5: Share your information and get a share code

  1. Select Share my information.
  2. Read the declaration and confirm you agree.
  3. Enter your name, job title, work email address and postal address.
  4. Select Confirm and get share code.

The platform displays a share code, and you can also download a supplier information file. As the factsheet explains, you then enter the share code in the buyer's e-tendering system or send it to the buyer, depending on what the tender documents ask for.

Example (illustration only): a two-person cleaning company in Leeds with a Companies House number registers in Step 3 and gets its PPON. It completes Step 4 over an evening using its latest accounts. When a council tender asks for "your CDP share code", it does Step 5 and pastes the code into the council's portal.

How to Find Your Tender ID Number

Every Find a Tender notice has a notice identifier shown on the notice and in search results, in the format NNNNNN-YYYY. A procurement can include several notices, so each procurement also has a procurement identifier (OCID), which starts with ocds-.

These are the two IDs you'll come across:

IDWhat it identifiesReal example from FTSWhere you see it
Notice identifierOne published notice099721-2026 (a UK7 contract details notice) (FTS search)In search results, on the notice and in the notice URL (/Notice/099721-2026)
Procurement identifier (OCID)The whole procurement, across all its noticesocds-h6vhtk-050108 (TfL procurement page)Labelled "Procurement identifier (OCID)" on the procurement page

The same TfL procurement page lists a UK2 preliminary market engagement notice and a UK4 tender notice under one OCID. If you're asking a buyer about "the tender", quote the OCID together with the notice identifier of the notice you're responding to.

To find an ID:

  1. Open Find a Tender search.
  2. Type a keyword, or paste an ID you already have into Keywords. That field searches "titles, descriptions, identifiers, and organization names".
  3. Open the notice and copy the identifier from the notice or from the browser address bar.

A common mistake is quoting your PPON when a buyer asks for the tender reference, or quoting the tender reference when they ask for your PPON. The notice ID identifies their opportunity. The PPON identifies your organisation.

Find a Tender Registration Number: What It Is and Where to See It

Your Find a Tender registration number is your PPON (Public Procurement Organisation Number). It's a 12-character code in groups separated by hyphens, such as EFGH-1234-IJKL. It identifies your organisation to public buyers. It is not a tracker for your bids (Tender Solutions guide).

The platform issues it once you save your organisation in Step 3. The official short guide describes it as a unique organisation identifier to share with contracting authorities before contract award (short guide). Bids aren't submitted or tracked inside Find a Tender. You submit them through each buyer's own tendering system.

To see your PPON (Tender Solutions):

  1. Sign in to Find a Tender.
  2. Go to My Account, then Your organisation.
  3. Select Registered organisation details.
  4. Look under Organisation identification.

Your PPON stays the same from one tender to the next. Your share code is generated each time you complete Share my information. If a buyer's form asks for both, put the PPON in the organisation ID field and the share code where it asks for CDP information.

Pitfall: some councils now ask existing suppliers for their PPON to update vendor records. Warwickshire County Council is one example. If you haven't registered yet, this request is a sign to do Steps 1 to 3 now, even if you have no tender in view.

Find a Tender Registration Number vs Companies House Number: What's the Difference?

A PPON identifies your organisation in public procurement. A Companies House number identifies a company on the official register at Find and update company information. One can't stand in for the other.

PPON (Find a Tender)Companies House number
Issued byFind a Tender / Central Digital Platform (Cabinet Office)Companies House
Who gets oneEvery registered supplier and buyerIncorporated companies and LLPs only
Sole tradersYes, once registered on FTSNo
CharitiesYesOnly if incorporated as a company
Used forIdentifying you on tenders and noticesYour legal company identity, filings and public record
Where to check itMy Account > Your organisation > Registered organisation detailsSearch your company name on the Companies House service
CostFree (factsheet)Separate from FTS

Pitfalls:

  • Treating them as interchangeable. Your Companies House number is used to set up your FTS organisation in Step 3, but buyers asking for a "PPON" want the code from FTS.
  • Assuming you can't register without a Companies House number. The question "Do you have a Companies House number?" includes a No option. Sole traders and unincorporated charities can still register. Charities can use a Charity Commission or Scottish Charity Regulator number. If you have no registry number at all, the platform assigns an identifier (short guide).
  • Mismatched names. Enter the registered name exactly as it appears on your official record. Buyers' due diligence checks can flag differences.

How to Use Find a Tender to Search and Bid on Contracts

You use Find a Tender to find and read notices, and then submit your bid through whichever portal the buyer names in the notice. The search filters let you narrow results by stage, notice type, CPV code, location, value, suitability and dates (FTS search).

Steps

  1. Open Find a Tender search.
  2. Under Procurement Stage, choose Open opportunities. This hides awards and contract notices you can't bid for.
  3. Under Notice Type, tick UK4: Tender notice for live tenders. Add UK2: Preliminary market engagement notice if you want early warning of contracts before they open. Notices under the Act are numbered UK1 to UK17. Older ones use F and T codes.
  4. Add an Industry CPV Code for your trade, and a Contract Location.
  5. Set Value minimum and maximum. You can choose whether the figures include or exclude VAT.
  6. Under Suitability, tick SMEs or VCSEs.
  7. Use Date Range to set a closing date at least two to three weeks away so you have time to write the bid.
  8. Once you're signed in, save the search and switch on email notifications (Find a Tender).
  9. Open the notice and look for the submission instructions. The documents and the bid itself are often handled in the buyer's own system. On the TfL procurement mentioned earlier, documents are released through TfL's Ariba sourcing event once you've been added as a bidder (TfL notice).
  10. Register on that buyer portal, then add your CDP share code where it's requested.

Pitfalls

  • Expecting an "Apply" button on Find a Tender. FTS doesn't take bids. Read the notice to find out where submissions go.
  • Leaving portal registration until the last day. Some buyer portals need manual approval before they let you in, as the TfL example shows. Register as soon as you decide to bid.
  • Skipping market engagement notices. UK2 notices are your chance to influence a specification before the tender opens.

If a notice points to a framework or a dynamic purchasing system, read Framework Agreement How to Get On or Dynamic Purchasing System: 6 SME Steps before you apply. Most tender notices lead to a Procurement Act selection stage, and Selection Questionnaire Procurement Act 2023: 7 SME Steps covers how to fill it in.

Find a Tender Buyer Registration: How It Differs From Supplier Sign-Up

Buyer registration is for contracting authorities that publish notices. It begins with the same GOV.UK One Login, but you choose Buyer and then wait for the application to be verified before you can publish anything. Suppliers can carry on immediately.

Supplier registrationBuyer registration
WhoBusinesses, sole traders, charities, social enterprisesContracting authorities (councils, NHS bodies, central government, universities and others)
Organisation type chosenSupplierBuyer
After savingPPON issued; carry on to Supplier Information"Application Pending" may show until the system verifies it (CPC guidance)
Main outputsPPON, share code, supplier information fileAbility to publish notices; buyers also get a unique identifier
When neededWhen you want to bidBefore the first notifiable procurement under the Act (CPC)

An organisation can be both. The homepage says an account can "register a buyer or supplier organisation" (Find a Tender). For example, a housing association or a university might buy services and also sell them to other public bodies. If yours does both, register a separate Supplier organisation. Don't try to bid from a Buyer record.

Typical mistake: a supplier picks Buyer in Step 3 because they're "looking to buy into" a contract, and then waits on a pending approval that never applies to them. The fix is to register again and choose Supplier.

Tender Registration Meaning: Key Terms Explained

In procurement, "tender registration" means setting up an account and organisation profile so buyers can identify you and you can take part in bids. It isn't a licence to trade, and it isn't a quality accreditation.

Terms you'll come across:

  • Supplier registration (CDP/FTS): your organisation record on Find a Tender. It's free and done once.
  • PPON: your organisation's unique procurement identifier, in a format such as EFGH-1234-IJKL.
  • Supplier Information: the six sections (Basic Information to Financial Information) that buyers rely on instead of asking the same questions on every tender.
  • Share code: what you hand to a buyer so they can see your Supplier Information.
  • Buyer portal registration: a separate account on the buyer's own e-tendering system, where you actually submit the bid.
  • Notice identifier / OCID: the IDs for the opportunity, not for you.

Pitfalls:

  • "Registered" doesn't mean "approved". Buyers still assess you against their own conditions and the exclusion grounds in each procurement.
  • Registration doesn't win work. It gets you in the door. Price, quality and social value answers decide the outcome. See Social Value in Tenders: PPN 002.
  • Out-of-date Supplier Information. If your directors, address or accounts change, update the record before your next share code, because the code shares whatever is saved at that point.

Next steps

You can have your PPON today and a share code ready before your next bid.

What to do yourself today:

  1. Choose your Administrator and a shared tenders email address. Then do Steps 1 to 3 on Find a Tender and write your PPON down where your team can find it.
  2. Collect what Step 4 needs: your latest accounts, the details of the people who control the organisation, and any qualifications or trade assurances. Complete Complete Supplier Information in one go.
  3. Set up a saved search: Open opportunities, UK4 and UK2 notices, your CPV code and region, and the SME or VCSE suitability filter. Then switch on email notifications.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: the official route costs £0. Find a Tender doesn't offer a paid plan (as of October 2026; check the CDP factsheet). For free official help, the Cabinet Office has published walkthrough videos, including "A guide for suppliers: How to register an organisation and the first administrator in 3 easy steps", and the Contact us page on Find a Tender handles account problems. Independent bid consultants will also complete the registration and Supplier Information for you. They set their own fees, so ask for a fixed written quote before agreeing. Paying someone makes sense if you have a lot of connected persons or a complicated group structure. It doesn't make sense if all you need is the Step 1 to 3 setup, which is free and takes one sitting. Whoever does the work, the declaration in Step 5 is yours, so check every answer before you confirm it.

Related guides on this site:

  • Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender: 2026 Table and Steps
  • How to Win Government Contracts UK: 7 Steps for SMEs (2026)
  • Selection Questionnaire Procurement Act 2023: 7 SME Steps

FAQ

Is Find a Tender registration free?

Yes. GOV.UK says "Find a Tender is free to use for everyone. There are no charges and you should not pay to view opportunities" (factsheet). Creating your One Login, registering, getting a PPON and generating share codes are all free.

Do I need a Companies House number to register on Find a Tender?

No. If you answer No to "Do you have a Companies House number?", the platform offers alternatives such as a Charity Commission or Scottish Charity Regulator number. If none of those apply, it assigns you an identifier (short guide).

Can sole traders and charities register on Find a Tender?

Yes. Both register as a Supplier in the same way as a limited company. A charity uses its regulator number where it has one, and a sole trader usually gets a platform-assigned identifier. When you complete your details you can say whether you are an SME or a VCSE.

What happens after I register as a supplier on Find a Tender?

You get a PPON straight away and can complete the six Supplier Information sections. After that you select Share my information to get a share code for each bid (GOV.UK guide). Bids still go through each buyer's own portal.

Is Find a Tender the same as Contracts Finder?

No. New procurements under the Procurement Act 2023, from 24 February 2025, publish their notices on Find a Tender. Contracts Finder still holds procurements that started under the older rules (Contracts Finder transparency guidance). Our Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender guide has a side-by-side table.
