item.title: Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender: 2026 Table and Steps
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender in 2026: which UK site lists which contracts, the £12,000/£30,000 and £135,018 thresholds, and how SMEs register and search.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

In 2026, check Find a Tender first. Since 24 February 2025, every new UK public procurement under the Procurement Act 2023 has been published on Find a Tender, whether it sits above or below threshold. Contracts Finder is now mainly for older procurements that started under the previous rules and for looking up past contract awards in England. Under the Act, Contracts Finder is no longer a required place to publish (PPN 019 guidance). Both sites are free. You can search either one without an account. To bid on Procurement Act tenders, though, you will need a Find a Tender supplier registration.

Which option is right for you?

Start with Find a Tender unless you have a specific reason to look at older or regional records.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner who has never bidFind a Tender. It is the one place all new notices must appearFind a Tender search, then Opportunities
You bid every week (daily work use)A Find a Tender saved search with email alerts, plus a monthly look at Contracts FinderFind a Tender search results → Save search
Zero budgetBoth. Neither costs anything to useCentral Digital Platform factsheet
Researching what buyers paid beforeContracts Finder, using the Awarded contract stageContracts Finder search
Charity or social enterpriseFind a Tender with the VCSE suitability filterFind a Tender search results
Based in Scotland, Wales or Northern IrelandFind a Tender plus your devolved portalGOV.UK Contracts Finder page (lists the regional sites)

Why it works this way: the government says that procurements "whether above or below threshold commenced from 24 February 2025 only require notices to be published on FTS" (PPN 019 guidance). Contracts Finder still matters for history and for older procurements, but new opportunities have to appear on Find a Tender.

What Is Contracts Finder?

Contracts Finder is the government's older search service for public contracts in England. Since February 2025 it has mainly held procurements that started under the old rules, plus past awards.

The GOV.UK Contracts Finder page says you can use it to "search for contract opportunities in different sectors" and "look up details of previous tenders and contracts". It covers contracts worth over £12,000 including VAT. Under the Public Contracts Regulations 2015 (PCR 2015), central government bodies had to publish there above £12,000, and sub-central bodies, NHS trusts and NHS foundation trusts above £30,000 (PPN 019 guidance). Bodies whose functions are wholly or mainly Scottish, Welsh or Northern Irish were exempt, which is why it is effectively an England service.

The rules for Contracts Finder are now different. PPN 019 was updated on 31 March 2025 (update note). It says no new procurements can be run under PCR 2015 after 24 February 2025. Procurements that started before then must keep following PCR 2015 until the contract ends, and their notices still go on Contracts Finder. So you will still see award notices and some later-stage activity there. Brand-new opportunities, however, are only required on Find a Tender.

Example (illustrative): A council started a cleaning contract under PCR 2015 in January 2025 and awards it in spring 2026. That award notice belongs on Contracts Finder. A new cleaning contract the same council advertises in 2026 is run under the Procurement Act 2023 and must go on Find a Tender.

Pitfalls:

  • Out-of-date threshold on GOV.UK. The Contracts Finder start page still says high-value contracts are "usually above £139,688 including VAT" (GOV.UK). That was the old central government figure. Since 1 January 2026 it has been £135,018 (see the threshold section below).
  • Treating Contracts Finder as complete. If Contracts Finder is the only place you search in 2026, you will miss new below-threshold tenders that buyers are only required to publish on Find a Tender.

What Is Find a Tender (Service)?

Find a Tender (sometimes called Find a Tender Service or FTS) is the UK's central digital platform for public procurement. All UK contracting authorities now publish their procurement notices there.

It replaced the EU's Tenders Electronic Daily (TED) for UK notices on 31 December 2020 (Find a Tender home page). An enhanced version went live on 24 February 2025 as the "central digital platform" required by the Procurement Act 2023. GOV.UK describes it as the place "where all UK contracting authorities publish information relating to procurement" (Central Digital Platform factsheet).

It does two jobs for suppliers:

  1. Finding notices. Pipeline notices, tender notices, award notices, contract details notices, framework and dynamic market notices, and even payment compliance data.
  2. Holding your supplier information. You enter your organisation's details once and then share them with buyers using a share code, so you don't retype the same core details for every bid.

The factsheet is clear on cost: "Find a Tender is free to use for everyone. There are no charges and you should not pay to view opportunities in the public sector."

Notice codes are worth learning because they appear on every listing (notice types page):

CodeNoticeWhat it means for you
UK1Pipeline noticePlanned spending. Early warning only
UK3Planned procurement noticeA tender is coming. It can shorten the later bidding window to as little as 10 days
UK4Tender noticeLive opportunity. Above and below threshold
UK6Contract award noticeWinner chosen. The standstill period starts
UK7Contract details noticeContract signed. Required for below-threshold contracts too

Pitfalls:

  • Assuming FTS is only for big contracts. The Find a Tender home page still points smaller buyers towards Contracts Finder, but for Procurement Act procurements the below-threshold tender notice (UK4) has to be published on the central digital platform "before being published elsewhere" (below-threshold guidance).
  • Expecting to submit your bid on FTS. You don't. You get your share code from FTS and then bid "in the way that was determined by the buyer in the tender notice", usually on the buyer's own e-tendering portal (factsheet).

Contracts Finder vs Find a Tender: Which One Should You Check First?

Give each site a different job: Find a Tender for live bids and early warnings (UK1, UK3 and UK4 notices), and Contracts Finder for award research and legacy PCR 2015 activity.

The plan for many SME guides written before 2025 was "Contracts Finder for small, Find a Tender for big". That split no longer matches the law. Here is the side-by-side comparison as of October 2026:

Find a TenderContracts Finder
Legal role nowCentral digital platform under the Procurement Act 2023Publication platform for procurements started under PCR 2015
New opportunities since 24 Feb 2025Yes, above and below thresholdNot required under the Act
GeographyWhole UKEngland and non-devolved bodies
Lowest notice value£12,000 (central government) / £30,000 (other authorities), incl. VAT, for below-threshold noticesOver £12,000 incl. VAT
Above-threshold contractsYes (e.g. £135,018 central goods/services from 1 Jan 2026)Legacy PCR awards only
Account needed to searchNoNo
Account needed to bidSupplier registration and share code (under the Act)Not for searching. Bidding follows the buyer's instructions
Saved searches / email alertsYes, with an accountYes, with an account
SME / VCSE filterYes (Suitability)Not on the main search form
CostFreeFree

Sources: PPN 019 guidance, below-threshold guidance, GOV.UK Contracts Finder, Find a Tender search, Contracts Finder search.

A simple routine that covers both:

  1. Daily or weekly: read your Find a Tender saved-search emails. Open any UK4 tender notice that matches your work.
  2. Weekly: scan Find a Tender for UK1 pipeline and UK3 planned procurement notices from buyers you want to work with. They tell you what is coming months ahead.
  3. Monthly: search Contracts Finder with Procurement stage set to Awarded contract for your keywords. This shows who won similar work and roughly at what value.
  4. If you trade in Scotland, Wales or Northern Ireland: also check the devolved portals listed on the GOV.UK Contracts Finder page.

Buyers can also skip advertising completely. There is no requirement to publish a below-threshold tender notice when the buyer invites quotes from a closed group of pre-selected suppliers and doesn't advertise in any other way (below-threshold guidance). Neither site will show you those. Getting onto frameworks and buyers' supplier lists is how you reach that work. Our guide on how to get on a framework agreement covers it.

Find a Tender and Contracts Finder: Do I Need to Register for Both?

No. They are separate systems with separate accounts. For most SMEs in 2026, the Find a Tender supplier registration is the one that matters.

Neither site makes you register just to search. GOV.UK says of Contracts Finder: "You can still search and apply for contracts without an account". An account gives you email updates and saved searches (GOV.UK). On Find a Tender, suppliers "only need to register at the point that they want to bid for a contract" (factsheet). That said, it's sensible to register before a deadline is close.

Registering on Find a Tender (three official steps)

These steps follow the GOV.UK guide Suppliers: how to register your organisation and first administrator on Find a Tender in three easy steps:

  1. Create your sign-in. On Find a Tender, choose Sign in or register an account, then Create your GOV.UK One Login. Enter your work email and the 6-digit code sent to it. Then set a password and choose text message or an authenticator app for security codes (GOV.UK registration user guide).
  2. Register the organisation. Select Register an organisation, then choose Supplier. Have your Companies House number or Charity Commission number and registered address ready. If you don't have either number, the platform generates a unique identifier for you.
  3. Complete Supplier Information. On your organisation page, select Complete Supplier Information and fill in the sections: Basic Information, Connected Persons, Qualifications, Trade Assurances, Exclusions and Financial Information. In Basic Information you declare whether you are an SME, VCSE or public mutual.
  4. Get your share code. Select Share my information, then Create a share code. Tick the declaration and enter your name, job title, work email and postal address. Then choose Confirm and get share code. You can also download your supplier information file.

You give that share code to the buyer inside their tendering portal, or attach the downloaded file if they ask for it. If you need help with the questionnaire stage that follows, see our Selection Questionnaire guide for the Procurement Act 2023.

Registering on Contracts Finder

This is optional. Create an account from the Contracts Finder header if you want saved searches and email updates (GOV.UK). Older PCR procurements will still direct you to the buyer's own portal to bid.

Common registration mistakes and fixes

  • Using a personal email. The guide asks for your individual work email. If someone leaves, an admin linked to a personal Gmail account causes trouble. Fix: register with a work address and add a second administrator.
  • Leaving Supplier Information half-finished. You can't create a share code until the questionnaire is complete. Fix: finish it during a quiet week, not the night before a deadline.
  • Expecting old saved searches to vanish. If you used the old Find a Tender, saved searches carry over when you use the same email address (factsheet). Fix: sign in with the same email rather than making a new account.
  • Sole traders worried they can't register. No Companies House number is needed. The platform issues a unique identifier when neither a Companies House nor a Charity Commission number applies.

What Are the Current Thresholds for Find a Tender vs Contracts Finder?

From 1 January 2026, contracts above £135,018 (central government) or £207,720 (other authorities) for goods and services are "above threshold". Below-threshold notices apply from £12,000 or £30,000. All figures include VAT.

The thresholds come from the Procurement Act 2023 (Threshold Amounts) (Amendment) Regulations 2025, announced in PPN 023 (published 27 November 2025). The GOV.UK thresholds guidance confirms values are estimated "including VAT".

Contract type (as of October 2026)Before 1 Jan 2026From 1 Jan 2026
Goods/services, central government£139,688£135,018
Goods/services, sub-central (councils, NHS trusts, universities etc.)£214,904£207,720
Works£5,372,609£5,193,000
Light touch services (e.g. many health, social and education services)£663,540£663,540
Utilities (goods/services)£429,809£415,440
Defence and security (goods/services)£429,809£415,440
Below-threshold notice, central government—£12,000
Below-threshold notice, other authorities—£30,000

Sources: PPN 023, Blake Morgan summary of old and new values, below-threshold guidance.

How to use these numbers when choosing what to bid for:

  • £12,000/£30,000 to the upper threshold: "regulated below-threshold" territory. Buyers here "cannot restrict the submission of tenders by reference to suppliers' suitability". In other words, no pre-tender test of your legal status, financial capacity or technical ability (below-threshold guidance). For a new SME this is often the most realistic band.
  • Above threshold: fuller procedures and conditions of participation. The minimum tendering period is normally 25 days with electronic submission, or as few as 10 days if a UK3 notice went out 40 days to a year earlier (notice types). Below-threshold contracts have no set minimum.

Example (illustrative): A district council wants a £60,000 (incl. VAT) website rebuild. That is above £30,000 but below £207,720, so it should appear on Find a Tender as a below-threshold UK4 tender notice, with no pass/fail financial checks before tendering.

How to Search for Contracts on Contracts Finder (Step-by-Step)

Open Contracts Finder, enter keywords, set Contract location and Procurement stage, then save the search through your account to get email updates.

The search form at contractsfinder.service.gov.uk/Search is simpler than Find a Tender's. These are the labels as they appear on the page:

  1. In Keywords, type your service in plain words, e.g. "grounds maintenance" or "translation". The field searches contract title, description and buyer.
  2. Under Contract location, choose a Region or enter a Postcode.
  3. Under Procurement stage, tick what you need: Early engagement, Future opportunity, Opportunity or Awarded contract.
  4. Select Search. Use Reset to start again.
  5. If you have an account, save the search to get email updates (GOV.UK).

The most useful search in 2026 is Awarded contract. For example: if you run a small catering business in Yorkshire, search "catering" with the Yorkshire and the Humber region and Awarded contract ticked. You'll see which schools, councils or NHS bodies bought catering, roughly what they paid, when the contracts run until and, under PPN 019, often whether the winner was an SME or VCSE. A contract ending next year is an opportunity you can prepare for now.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Ticking only Opportunity and finding very little. That is expected for new work, which now goes to Find a Tender. Fix: run the same keywords on Find a Tender.
  • Ignoring Early engagement. These notices invite market engagement before a tender. Fix: answer them. Buyers often use the replies to shape lot sizes, which can make contracts easier for SMEs to win.

How to Search for Contracts on Find a Tender (Step-by-Step)

Open Find a Tender's search, filter by Industry CPV code, Contract location, Value and Suitability, then select Save search to get emails.

Go to Find a Tender search results. The filter labels below match the live page:

  1. Keywords: searches titles, descriptions, identifiers and organisation names. Start broad, e.g. "cleaning".
  2. Procurement stage: choose Open opportunities only for live bids. Add Pipeline and Planning if you want early warning of future tenders.
  3. Notice type: narrow down to the codes you care about, such as UK4 tender notices.
  4. Industry CPV code: pick the Common Procurement Vocabulary codes for your trade. Buyers tag notices with these, so they catch listings your keywords miss.
  5. Contract location: use Select regions for where you can actually deliver.
  6. Value: set a minimum and maximum. For example, £10,000 to £150,000 if you are a small firm that can't carry a large contract.
  7. Suitability: tick SME and/or VCSE. Buyers mark notices they consider suitable for smaller suppliers.
  8. Date range: filter by Publication date or Closing date.
  9. Select Update results, then use Sort results → Closing (first) so urgent deadlines come first.
  10. Select Save search (you'll be asked to sign in). Name the search and choose how often you want notification emails (GOV.UK how-to guide).

If you want to browse rather than filter, the home page also offers Opportunities, Contracts and Commercial tools. Commercial tools covers frameworks and dynamic markets, and it is worth checking because many buyers order from these instead of running new tenders (Find a Tender home).

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • Relying on the SME filter alone. It depends on how the buyer filled in the notice, so some suitable contracts won't carry the flag. Fix: run a second saved search without it.
  • One CPV code only. Fix: add the parent code and two or three related codes.
  • Missing the window. Some above-threshold tenders can run for only 10 days. Fix: set alerts to the most frequent option you can handle and have your share code ready in advance.
  • Starting the bid too late on scoring. Above-threshold tenders usually weight quality and social value. See our guide to social value in tenders under PPN 002.

Is Finder.com Legit? (And How It Differs From Contracts Finder/Find a Tender)

Finder.com is a real, FCA-regulated consumer comparison site, but it has nothing to do with Contracts Finder or Find a Tender.

According to its About page, Finder was founded in Australia in 2006, is owned by Hive Empire Pty Ltd, and its UK arm (Finder.com Comparison UK Ltd) launched in February 2017. It compares products such as mortgages, credit cards, energy and share trading. It is "authorised and regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority (FRN 786446)" and earns commission from featured providers. It does not list public sector contracts.

How to tell the services apart:

  • The official tender services live on service.gov.uk domains: find-tender.service.gov.uk and contractsfinder.service.gov.uk. The starting pages are on gov.uk.
  • The official services never charge you to view opportunities. Find a Tender's factsheet says "you should not pay to view opportunities in the public sector" (factsheet).
  • Commercial "tender finder" or "deal finder" sites with similar names are separate businesses. Some repackage the free government data and charge for alerts or analysis. That is legal. Just know you're paying for convenience, not for access.

Pitfall: searching "contracts finder" and clicking an ad or a lookalike site. Fix: bookmark the two service.gov.uk addresses above and go to them directly.

Next steps

You can set up both services in under an hour today, and you don't need to spend anything.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Open Find a Tender, set Keywords, Contract location and Suitability: SME (or VCSE), and select Save search with email notifications.
  2. Start your Find a Tender supplier registration (three-step guide) and get as far as you can on Complete Supplier Information.
  3. On Contracts Finder, search your keywords with Awarded contract and note three buyers whose contracts end in the next 12–18 months.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: commercial tender-alert and bid-writing services exist. Check each provider's own page for what is included and what it costs. They suit firms bidding several times a month that would rather pay than filter alerts themselves. They suit very small or occasional bidders less well. The data comes from the same free government sources, and no paid service can make a buyer publish a contract or improve your odds of winning on its own. Before you pay anyone, compare what they offer with what the free saved searches already give you.

Related guides on this site:

  • How to win government contracts in the UK: 7 steps for SMEs
  • Selection Questionnaire under the Procurement Act 2023
  • How to get on a framework agreement
  • Social value in tenders: PPN 002 steps and examples

FAQ

Is finder.com legit?

Yes. Finder is a genuine comparison website, and its UK company is authorised and regulated by the FCA under FRN 786446 (Finder About page). It compares consumer financial products and has no connection to the government's Contracts Finder. For public contracts, use only the service.gov.uk sites.

Is deal finder legit?

"Deal finder" is a generic name used by various unrelated shopping and tender-alert businesses, so judge each one on its own. None of them is an official government procurement service. If a "finder" site asks you to pay just to see public sector opportunities, remember that Find a Tender is free and the government says you should not pay to view them (factsheet).

What is Find a Tender used for if I'm a sole trader?

You use it to find opportunities, especially below-threshold ones from £12,000 or £30,000 including VAT, and to hold the supplier information buyers need when you bid. You don't need a Companies House number, because the platform generates a unique identifier if you have none (GOV.UK registration guide). Regulated below-threshold tenders can't screen you out on financial or technical capacity before you tender, which helps small traders.

Can charities and social enterprises bid through Contracts Finder?

Yes. Contracts Finder is open to any supplier, and award notices there show whether the winner was an SME or VCSE (PPN 019 guidance). For new opportunities in 2026, though, search Find a Tender and use the VCSE suitability filter. Register there with your Charity Commission number.

item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: How to win government contracts in the UK without paid tools: 7 steps using Find a Tender, CPV codes and Contracts Finder, with 2026 thresholds for SMEs.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To win government contracts in the UK, first register for free on Find a Tender, the central digital platform. Then set up saved searches on your CPV codes and bid for small, local contracts where your evidence fits the published award criteria. Under the Procurement Act 2023, central government buyers must advertise contracts worth £12,000 or more including VAT, and other public bodies must advertise from £30,000 (GOV.UK below-threshold guidance). You can find most of these opportunities yourself, and searching, registering and alerts cost nothing (Central Digital Platform factsheet).

Which option is right for you?

Your starting point depends on how much time you have and whether you've bid before. Use this table to pick your first move.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Complete beginner, never bidFind a Tender search filtered by Suitability: SME and your regionFind a Tender search
Sole trader or micro business, low budgetBelow-threshold notices from councils, schools and NHS trusts (no pre-qualification allowed)Find a Tender search, filter Value max £207,720
Charity or social enterprise (VCSE)Suitability: VCSE filter, plus contracts reserved for SMEs/VCSEs under PPN 005PPN 005 guide
You already bid regularly (daily work use)Saved searches on CPV codes, with email notifications, plus a second search for awardsFind a Tender sign-in
Older contracts started before 24 Feb 2025Contracts Finder, which still carries legacy noticesContracts Finder search
You sell common goods/services to many buyersA dynamic purchasing system you can join at any timeGCA RM6237 Low Value Purchase System

Here's why each one comes first. The SME filter shows buyers who have flagged a contract as suitable for small firms. Below-threshold tenders can't screen you out on financial standing before you bid. VCSEs get access to reserved competitions. Saved searches replace daily manual checking. And a dynamic purchasing system (DPS), unlike a framework, has no closed application window.

What Government Contracts Can SMEs Actually Get in the UK?

SMEs can bid for almost any advertised UK public contract, and the most realistic wins sit below the procurement thresholds. Those contracts must still be published on Find a Tender once they pass £12,000 (central government) or £30,000 (other public bodies) including VAT (GOV.UK).

Contracts fall into two bands, and the band changes how you bid.

BandValue (incl. VAT, procurements started from 1 Jan 2026)Who typically buysWhat it means for you
Notifiable below-threshold£12,000+ (central gov) / £30,000+ (others), up to the thresholdCouncils, schools, NHS trusts, police, universitiesNo pre-qualification stage; simpler bids
Above threshold: central government supplies/services£135,018+Government departments, agenciesFull Procurement Act process; conditions of participation possible
Above threshold: sub-central supplies/services£207,720+Councils, NHS bodiesAs above
Light touch services (e.g. some health, social, education)£663,540+AllMore flexible procedures
Works£5,193,000+AllConstruction-scale projects

Threshold figures come from Bevan Brittan's summary of the 2026 threshold regulations (as of October 2026). They apply to procurements started on or after 1 January 2026. Earlier procurements use the old figures, e.g. £139,688 for central government.

The below-threshold band is where most SMEs should start. GOV.UK states that buyers running a regulated below-threshold contract "cannot restrict the submission of tenders by reference to suppliers' suitability". In practice, nobody can knock you out at a pre-qualification stage for lacking three years of accounts. The same guidance gives these contracts implied 30-day payment terms (section 88) (GOV.UK).

Where the notices live (as of October 2026):

  • Find a Tender is the central digital platform. Every procurement started under the Procurement Act 2023 on or after 24 February 2025 is published there, above and below threshold, except below-threshold notices in Scotland (GOV.UK below-threshold guidance; Find a Tender notice types).
  • Contracts Finder still carries notices from procurements that began under the old Public Contracts Regulations 2015, such as later stages and awards. It still has a Procurement Stage filter (Early engagement, Future opportunity, Opportunity, Awarded contract) and a postcode radius of 5–50 miles (Contracts Finder). Treat it as a second check, not your main feed.

A pitfall to avoid: not everything is advertised. A buyer doesn't have to publish a below-threshold notice if it only invites quotes from a closed group of pre-selected suppliers and doesn't advertise the work any other way (GOV.UK). The fix is to get onto those quote lists. Join a DPS such as RM6237 (see below), or register on the supplier portal of the councils you want to work with.

The 7 Steps to Win Your First Government Contract (Beginner's Guide)

Here's the beginner path in short: register once, find your CPV codes, save searches, then bid small and local before you try national frameworks. Each step below uses only free official services.

Step 1: Create a GOV.UK One Login. On Find a Tender, choose Sign in. Create a GOV.UK One Login with your work email, enter the six-digit code sent to you, and set up two-factor authentication on a mobile phone (Find a Tender; registration steps summarised from the GOV.UK supplier user guide).

Step 2: Register your organisation. Go to My Organisations → Register an organisation. Have these ready: your Companies House or Charity Commission number (if you have one), registered and postal address, VAT number (if registered), website and organisation type. If you don't have a registration number, as many sole traders don't, the platform can generate a unique identifier (supplier user guide).

Step 3: Complete your core supplier information. This covers basic details, SME/VCSE status, financial accounts, connected persons, qualifications and trade associations, and any exclusion grounds. When a buyer asks for it, generate a share code and paste it into their e-tendering system. It's free, and you won't have to re-enter the same details for every bid (CDP factsheet). You don't need to do this on day one. GOV.UK says suppliers can register "at the point that they want to bid". Still, finishing it before your first deadline saves stress.

Step 4: Pick 3–6 CPV codes. See the next section for how.

Step 5: Build and save searches. On the Find a Tender search page, set Industry CPV code, Contract location, Value (minimum and maximum) and Suitability (SME and/or VCSE). Then choose Save search and turn on email notifications (Find a Tender search results).

Step 6: Qualify each notice before you write anything. Open the UK4 tender notice and check the closing date, the value, the award criteria and weightings, and any mandatory requirements such as insurance levels. If you can't evidence at least one similar job, skip it and wait for the next one.

Step 7: Bid, then learn from the assessment summary. Under the Act, every supplier whose tender was assessed gets an assessment summary with scores and reasons for each criterion, plus the winner's scored information (redacted where needed) (GOV.UK e-learning Module 7; Procurement Pathway). Use it to rewrite your weakest answer before the next bid.

Example (illustrative): a two-person grounds maintenance firm in Leeds could save a search on CPV 77310000, with Contract location set to Yorkshire and the Humber, Value £30,000–£207,720 and Suitability: SME. That would surface council parks and school grounds contracts without manual browsing.

How to Find CPV Codes for Your Business (and Why They Matter)

CPV (Common Procurement Vocabulary) codes classify what's being bought. Saved searches built on the right codes are how you see relevant live tenders without searching by hand. Find a Tender's own filter describes CPV as the system "used to classify contracts in a standardised way" (Find a Tender).

Codes are hierarchical. The first two digits are the division and each further digit narrows it down. A broad code like 72000000 catches all IT services. A narrow one catches far fewer notices, and if the buyer tagged the contract at a different level, you can miss it.

How to find yours:

  1. Search the full code list on SIMAP's CPV page using plain words for what you sell, e.g. "cleaning" or "training".
  2. Cross-check against real notices. On Find a Tender, search a keyword, open 5–10 relevant notices, and note the CPV codes buyers actually used.
  3. Keep one broad code and two to five narrow codes. Then add a keyword search to catch buyers who mis-tag.
  4. Use Procurement stage: Award or Contract with the same codes to see who already holds the work and when it ends.
What you sell (examples)Example CPV codeDescription
Office/commercial cleaning90910000Cleaning services
Grounds maintenance77310000Planting and maintenance services of green areas
Catering55520000Catering services
Training courses80500000Training services
Marketing and design79340000Advertising and marketing services
IT support and software72000000IT services: consulting, software development, Internet and support
Community and care services (often VCSE)85300000Social work and related services
Building work45000000Construction work

Codes are taken from the CPV list on SIMAP. Check the exact wording there before you save a search.

A common mistake is choosing only the most specific code. If a council tags a cleaning contract as 90900000 (cleaning and sanitation services) and you only follow 90911200, you won't see it. Include the parent code in your search.

How to Write a Winning Bid Response (PQQ and ITT Basics)

Score against the published criteria, not against your brochure. Under the Act, buyers must publish award criteria that are "clear, measurable and specific" and show how much each one counts, through weightings, ranking or another method (GOV.UK Module 7).

The old terms still turn up. A PQQ (pre-qualification questionnaire) is now, above threshold, a set of conditions of participation answered through a selection questionnaire. The ITT (invitation to tender) is the tender documents themselves. For below-threshold contracts there's no pre-qualification stage, so you go straight to the tender response. Our Selection Questionnaire guide covers the above-threshold selection stage in detail.

A practical writing process:

  1. Build a scoring grid. List every question, its weighting and the word limit. Spend your time in proportion to the weighting. A question worth 30% deserves three times the effort of one worth 10%.
  2. Mirror the question's structure. If the question asks for "approach, resources and risk", use those three words as sub-headings in that order.
  3. Prove each claim. Give a named past job (with permission), dates, volumes and the result, e.g. "cleaned 4 primary schools, 2019–2025, no missed cleans reported". Swap "we are passionate about quality" for the process you actually follow.
  4. Answer the specification, not the sector. Copy the buyer's own terms: their site names, service hours, KPIs.
  5. Price exactly as instructed. Use their pricing schedule, check whether values are inclusive or exclusive of VAT, and don't add assumptions in a covering letter.
  6. Use clarification questions before the deadline the buyer sets. Answers are usually published to all bidders, so ask anything that changes how you'd price.
  7. Cover social value where it's scored. Central government contracts use the PPN 002 Social Value Model. See our social value answer examples.

The Act moved evaluation from "most economically advantageous tender" to "most advantageous tender", so cheapest doesn't automatically win (GOV.UK Module 7). If quality is weighted at 60% and price at 40%, a strong method statement can make up for a slightly higher price.

Example (illustrative): say a question asks how you'll handle staff absence, worth 15%. "We have a robust contingency plan" scores weakly. "Two trained relief staff within 25 miles, cover confirmed by 7am, and the buyer's site manager notified by text" gives the evaluator something they can score.

Tender periods are short, so plan backwards. The standard minimum for above-threshold competitive tenders is 25 days. That can drop to 10 days if the buyer published a qualifying planned procurement notice (UK3) or there's genuine urgency (Find a Tender notice types; GOV.UK competitive tendering guidance). That's why it pays to watch UK1 pipeline and UK3 planned procurement notices.

Which Government Contracts Are Easiest for New Suppliers to Win?

Lower-value contracts from councils, schools, NHS trusts and other local bodies are usually the most winnable. They're below threshold, they can't use pre-qualification, and they can be reserved for local SMEs and VCSEs. No contract is "easy", but competition and paperwork are lighter here than on national frameworks.

Under PPN 005 (updated February 2025), in-scope organisations may reserve below-threshold competitions by supplier location. They may also reserve them for SMEs and VCSEs, but only in combination with a location reservation. So a buyer can run a competition open only to SMEs based in a particular region.

RouteTypical competitionPaperworkLimitation
Below-threshold open tender (councils, schools, NHS trusts)Low to moderateTender response only; no suitability pre-screenValues are smaller; you still compete on quality and price
Reserved below-threshold competition (PPN 005)Lower, restricted to local/SME/VCSEAs aboveOnly where the buyer chooses to reserve; you must be based in the named area
Invited quotes from a DPS such as RM6237 Low Value Purchase SystemVaries; buyers filter by location and specialismJoin once, then respond to invitationsRuns to 31 March 2027 (as of October 2026; check the official page)
Subcontracting to a prime contractorDepends on the primeUsually lighterLower margin; payment flows through the prime
National framework (GCA)HighFull selection and tender stageFixed application windows; see below

Steps to find the easier ones on Find a Tender:

  1. Set Procurement stage to Open opportunities.
  2. Set Value maximum to £207,720, the sub-central threshold for procurements started from 1 January 2026.
  3. Tick Suitability: SME (and VCSE if relevant).
  4. Set Contract location to your region, then use Sort results → Closing (last first) so you see the notices that give you the most time.

This route doesn't suit everyone. If you need a single £1m+ contract to justify the bid cost, below-threshold work will feel small. If you can't show at least one comparable job, even low-value tenders will be hard to score well on. Some firms start with a private-sector or subcontract reference first, and that's a sensible order.

Do You Need to Register on a Framework Before Bidding?

No. Most tender notices on Find a Tender are open competitions anyone can bid on directly. Frameworks are a separate route where you compete once to become a pre-approved supplier, and buyers then call off work from that pool.

Crown Commercial Service became the Government Commercial Agency (GCA) on 1 April 2026. GCA lists four supply routes: frameworks, dynamic purchasing systems, dynamic markets and catalogues (GCA how to supply; GCA launch news). GCA says it connects suppliers to "20,000 UK public sector buyers spending over £37 billion a year" (GCA).

RouteCan you join any time?Best forWatch out for
Open tender (UK4 notice)Yes, while the notice is openFirst contracts, local workOne contract per bid
FrameworkNo, only during the tender windowFirms with references and capacityMiss the window and you wait until it's re-let
Dynamic purchasing system (legacy)Yes, during its lifeCommon goods/servicesBeing on it doesn't guarantee work
Dynamic market (Procurement Act 2023)Yes, during its lifeAs DPS, under the new ActSame: membership isn't a contract

On Find a Tender, the Commercial tool filter (Framework, Dynamic market, Utilities dynamic market, Dynamic purchasing system) shows these separately from one-off tenders (Find a Tender).

Here's the pitfall. Getting onto a framework takes effort and earns nothing until a buyer runs a call-off. Many SMEs win a framework place and then never receive a call-off. For a beginner, aim for open tenders first. Once you have two or three references, move on to frameworks using our framework agreement guide.

Common Mistakes That Get SME Bids Rejected

Missed deadlines, failed pass/fail requirements and generic answers lose more SME bids than price does. All three can be fixed before you submit.

  • Late or incomplete submission. E-tendering portals close at a fixed time, often midday, and won't accept a late upload. Fix: aim to submit 24 hours early, and check that every attachment has uploaded by viewing the submission summary.
  • Failing a pass/fail condition. Above threshold, conditions of participation can cover insurance levels, financial standing and technical ability. Fix: before writing, list every mandatory item in the tender documents and confirm you meet it. If a stated insurance level is out of reach, ask by clarification whether "willing to obtain on award" is acceptable.
  • Out-of-date core supplier information. Your share code reflects what's on the platform. Fix: update your details in Find a Tender (accounts, connected persons, exclusions) before each bid (CDP factsheet).
  • Generic, copy-pasted method statements. Evaluators score against the question, not the volume of text. Fix: reuse your evidence, but rewrite each answer around the buyer's specification and wording.
  • Pricing errors. Mixing up figures inclusive and exclusive of VAT, or leaving cells blank. Fix: complete the buyer's own pricing template and have a second person check the arithmetic.
  • Ignoring the assessment summary. Fix: compare your score for each criterion with the winner's, and rewrite the answer with the biggest gap.

Example (illustrative): a VCSE bidding for a £45,000 council youth service gives a strong answer, but it describes its work in general terms and doesn't name the council's three target wards. A competitor names them and scores higher on that criterion. Nothing about the service itself was different. The difference was how closely the answer fitted the specification.

What Happens After You Win a Government Contract?

Winning starts a formal sequence. Above threshold, it runs: assessment summary, then a UK6 contract award notice, then a standstill of at least 8 working days, then signature, then a UK7 contract details notice (Find a Tender notice types).

  1. Assessment summary. Every assessed bidder receives one before the award notice is published (GOV.UK Module 7).
  2. UK6 contract award notice. This starts the standstill period where one applies.
  3. Standstill period of at least 8 working days. The contract can't be signed until it ends. That gives unsuccessful bidders time to challenge (this replaced the old 10 calendar days). Use the time to line up staff, insurance and subcontractors. Don't start work yet.
  4. Contract signature and mobilisation. Agree start dates, contacts, KPIs and invoicing details such as purchase order numbers.
  5. UK7 contract details notice. Published within 30 days of signature for above-threshold contracts (120 days for light-touch). For contracts of £5 million or more, a redacted copy of the contract follows within 90 days (GOV.UK Module 7).
  6. Payment and performance. Public contracts carry implied 30-day payment terms: section 68 of the Act above threshold (legislation.gov.uk), section 88 below (GOV.UK). For larger contracts, buyers may publish performance (UK9-type) notices.

For below-threshold contracts, the buyer publishes a contract details notice, and a formal standstill isn't normally part of the process.

One planning tip: 30-day terms run from receipt of a valid, undisputed invoice. If cash flow is tight, find out on day one exactly what a valid invoice must include. A missing PO number is a common cause of delay.

Next steps

Do these today. You don't need a live opportunity to make progress.

  1. Create your GOV.UK One Login and register your organisation on Find a Tender. It's free, and it's the identity every Procurement Act bid will use.
  2. Pick three CPV codes (one broad, two narrow) from SIMAP. Save one Find a Tender search with Suitability: SME, your region and a £207,720 maximum value, and turn on email notifications.
  3. Save a second search with Procurement stage: Award on the same codes, so you can see who wins in your area and at what value.

If you'd rather not do it yourself: start with the free official option. GOV.UK publishes the official Procurement Act 2023 e-learning, and GCA has supplier guidance on how to supply. If you want structured bid-writing training, APMP Foundation is a recognised certification. BidCraft Academy, for example, lists the course alone at £211 and a non-member exam bundle at £770 (as of October 2026; check the official page) (BidCraft Academy). Membership of APMP is required to sit the exam. It suits people who'll write bids regularly or want a career in bid work. It doesn't suit a sole trader planning one or two small bids a year, who will get more from rewriting answers using assessment summaries. Freelance bid writers are another option, but their fees vary widely, and they still need your evidence and pricing to write a credible response.

Related guides on this site:

  • Selection Questionnaire Procurement Act 2023: 7 SME Steps
  • Framework Agreement How to Get On: 6 SME Steps (2026)
  • Social Value in Tenders: PPN 002 Steps and Answer Examples

FAQ

Do I need to be VAT registered to bid for government contracts?

Not as a general rule. Whether you must register for VAT depends on your taxable turnover under HMRC rules, not on who your customers are. The supplier registration on Find a Tender asks for a VAT number as part of basic information where you have one. Contract values in notices are shown including VAT, so check the pricing instructions in each tender to see how the buyer wants VAT handled.

How long do government tenders take to be awarded?

No single timescale applies. For above-threshold competitive tenders, the minimum tender period is usually 25 days, and evaluation takes however long the buyer needs. A standstill of at least 8 working days follows the award notice before signature (Find a Tender notice types). Many tender documents include an indicative timetable, so check it before you plan staffing.

Can a sole trader bid for government contracts?

Yes. Find a Tender registration works without a Companies House number, because the platform can generate a unique identifier for organisations that don't have one. Below-threshold contracts are especially accessible because buyers can't pre-screen suppliers on suitability (GOV.UK). Make sure you can meet any insurance or capacity requirements stated in the tender.

Is there a free alert system for new government tenders?

Yes. Find a Tender lets signed-in users save search criteria and sign up for email notifications at no cost (Find a Tender). GOV.UK states that you "should not pay to view opportunities in the public sector" (CDP factsheet).

item.title: Framework Agreement How to Get On: 6 SME Steps (2026)
item.dc:creator: Aoba Works
item.description: Framework agreement how to get on: 6 steps from Find a Tender registration to call-off wins, plus how open frameworks and dynamic markets reopen for SMEs.
item.content:encoded:
How this guide was made: drafted with AI assistance from the official sources linked below, then passed an automated editorial check before publishing. Our process

To get on a framework agreement, first register your organisation on Find a Tender and complete your supplier information. Then find a framework or dynamic market that is open to bids, meet its conditions of participation, and send a compliant tender before the deadline. If you miss a closed framework, you have to wait for its replacement. Under the Procurement Act 2023, open frameworks must reopen to new suppliers within three years, and dynamic markets accept applications at any time.

Which option is right for you?

Your best first move depends on how ready you are to bid and how much time you can give it each week.

Your situationWhat to pick firstFirst page to open
Beginner, never bid for public workRegister on Find a Tender and complete your supplier information before you look for frameworksFind a Tender registration guide (GOV.UK)
Small firm or sole trader with no public sector track recordA dynamic market, because you can apply at any timeGCA: How to supply through dynamic markets
Bids are part of your daily work and you want national reachWatch the GCA pipeline for frameworks opening in the next 6–12 monthsGCA upcoming agreements
Local service provider (care, cleaning, grounds, training)Council and NHS opportunities under the threshold, plus local frameworksContracts Finder
Tight budget, no bid writerFree official routes only. Use the buyer's clarification process instead of paid helpGCA: Find tender opportunities
Based in Scotland, Wales or Northern IrelandYour devolved portal as well as Find a TenderPublic Contracts Scotland, Sell2Wales, eTendersNI (listed on GCA's opportunities page)

Why these picks: a dynamic market removes the biggest timing risk for a new supplier, because you can't miss its window. A national framework is worth chasing only if you can deliver across the regions or lots it covers.

What is a framework agreement and why does it matter for SMEs?

A framework agreement is a pre-agreed list of suppliers and terms. Public bodies use it to award contracts ("call-offs") without running a full new tender each time. For an SME, a place on a framework means you can win repeat public sector work without starting from zero for every contract.

The framework itself usually comes with no promise of work. It sets the rules: who the suppliers are, which lots they cover, the core contract terms and how future contracts get awarded. Buyers then use it when they need something. The Government Commercial Agency (GCA) runs many of the best-known national frameworks. It replaced Crown Commercial Service (CCS) on 1 April 2026, and existing frameworks, supplier listings and call-off contracts continued unchanged.

Two official numbers show both the opportunity and the catch:

  • When Digital Outcomes and Specialists 5 opened, 3,340 suppliers were awarded places, and 94% of them were SMEs (GCA).
  • In CCS's 2025 SME action plan, SMEs made up about 75% of suppliers on CCS agreements but received just under 11% of direct spend (Ward Hadaway summary of the CCS SME action plan).

That gap is the most important thing to understand before you start. Getting on a framework is a qualification. The revenue comes from winning call-offs afterwards (see the mini-competition section below).

For example, a 12-person IT support firm might win a place on a regional lot of a technology framework. Over the next year, three councils could invite every supplier in that lot to quote for specific projects. The firm earns money only from the quotes it wins.

How to get on a framework agreement: the 6 steps

Getting on a framework takes six steps: register, find the right notice, check the conditions, prepare your evidence, submit a compliant tender, then win work once you're admitted. Most rejections happen in steps 3 to 5, so plan most of your time there.

Step 1: Register on Find a Tender (once, free)

Find a Tender is the central digital platform under the Procurement Act 2023. It stores your core supplier information, and you can reuse that for every bid. It costs nothing to use, and the government says you should not pay to view public sector opportunities.

The official three-step guide uses these labels:

  1. Choose Create your GOV.UK One Login (or Sign in if you already have one), then Register an organisation. Have ready a work email, your Companies House number or equivalent (a Charity Commission number, for example), your registered address and a shared organisation email. If you have no registry number, for example as a sole trader, the service generates a unique identifier for you.
  2. Choose Complete Supplier Information and fill in each section: Basic Information, Connected Persons, Qualifications, Trade Assurances, Exclusions and Financial Information.
  3. Choose Share my information, then Create a share code. Agree to the declaration, give your name, job title, work email and postal address, then choose Confirm and get share code.

Buyers will ask for this share code in their own tender portal. The factsheet says you might paste it into the buyer's eSender system or email the downloaded file, depending on what the tender documents say.

Step 2: Find the notice and register on the buyer's portal

Frameworks are advertised with a tender notice on Find a Tender (see the next section for other places to look). Each buyer then runs the competition on its own eSourcing system. GCA, for example, says it runs all GCA procurements through its eSourcing portal. You register there, express interest and download the invitation to tender. Register on the portal days before the deadline, not hours. New accounts sometimes need verification.

Step 3: Read the conditions of participation and the lots

Open the tender documents and find three things: the lots (by region or service), the conditions of participation (financial, technical, legal), and the evaluation criteria with their weightings. If you can't meet a mandatory condition for a lot, don't bid for that lot.

Step 4: Prepare your evidence pack

Gather your accounts, insurance details, references or case studies, policies and the named people who will deliver the work. The documents section below lists what's usually asked for.

Step 5: Submit a compliant tender

GCA frameworks use a Procurement Specific Questionnaire (PSQ) to check you meet the conditions of participation. After that come quality questions and pricing (GCA). Answer every question, follow the word limits and upload the pricing schedule in the format they give you.

Step 6: Get admitted, then win call-offs

If you're successful, you're awarded a place on the framework. GCA warns that registering and expressing interest "does not guarantee success". Even after you're admitted, you still have to win work through mini-competitions or direct awards.

Common mistakes at this stage, and how to fix them:

  • You register on Find a Tender but never generate a share code. Fix: finish step 3 of the registration and save the code where your bid team can find it.
  • Your supplier information is out of date. Fix: update it whenever directors, owners or accounts change, then make a new share code.
  • You bid for every lot. Fix: bid only where you can deliver at the stated volume and in the stated area.

Where to find live framework opportunities for SMEs

Find a Tender lists framework notices above the threshold. Contracts Finder covers lower-value work in England. GCA's pipeline shows national frameworks before they open, and devolved portals cover Scotland, Wales and Northern Ireland.

Above-threshold procurements have to follow the full rules of the Act. From 1 January 2026, the thresholds including VAT are £135,018 for central government goods and services, £207,720 for councils, the NHS and other sub-central bodies, and £5,193,000 for works (Burges Salmon; as of October 2026, check GOV.UK for updates). Below that, a contract is "notifiable" and published on Contracts Finder from £12,000 for central government and £30,000 for other authorities, including VAT (Hempsons).

WhereWhat you'll findBest forLimitation
Find a TenderFramework, open framework and dynamic market notices above threshold, UK-wideAnyone targeting larger frameworksSearch results are long; you need filters by CPV code and region
Contracts FinderContracts from £12k/£30k in EnglandSmall and local suppliersFew frameworks; mainly one-off contracts
GCA upcoming agreementsNational frameworks due to openFirms that can plan 6–12 months aheadOnly covers GCA, not councils or the NHS
Devolved portals (Public Contracts Scotland, Sell2Wales, eTendersNI)Devolved and local bodiesSuppliers based in those nationsSeparate registration for each
Council, NHS and university procurement pagesLocal frameworks and supplier daysLocal service SMEsEvery buyer's site is different; you have to check them yourself

GCA's own opportunities page also suggests approaching the procurement teams of councils, the NHS and universities directly, because those bodies manage their own suppliers.

Here's an example search routine. Once a week, filter Find a Tender for the notice types tender notice and dynamic market notice in your service category. Check Contracts Finder for your county. Check the GCA pipeline once a month.

Framework agreement vs dynamic purchasing system (DPS): which should SMEs apply to?

Frameworks usually close after their first tender window, while a DPS, and now a dynamic market, stays open for new suppliers to join at any time. That makes a dynamic market the easier way in for newer or smaller SMEs. Since the Act came in, new DPSs are no longer set up. Dynamic markets replace them.

Under the transitional rules, a DPS whose procurement started before 24 February 2025 is deemed to end on 23 February 2029 at the latest, while frameworks set up under the old rules can run to their agreed end date (Birketts). So you'll still see some old DPSs for now, but new ones will be dynamic markets.

FeatureClosed frameworkOpen frameworkDynamic market
When you can joinOnly at the first tenderAt the first tender and each reopeningAny time
Maximum termGenerally 4 years (8 for defence and security or utilities) (GOV.UK)8 years in total (s.49)Set by the buyer
Entry testFull tender with quality and priceFull tender at each reopeningConditions for membership only
Supplier numbersFixed at awardCan grow at reopeningNo maximum
FeesOnly on call-offs you win, as a fixed %SameOnly on contracts you win, as a fixed % (GOV.UK)

Choose a dynamic market if you're new, cash-tight or not sure about your timing. Membership checks your legal and financial capacity or technical ability. It isn't a scored contest against other bidders. GCA also says there are no joining fees, just a commission on sales you make through the agreement. The limitation is that, once you're in, you compete for every contract, often against a lot of members.

Choose a framework if the buyers you want use it and you can write strong quality answers. Fewer suppliers on a lot can mean better odds in each mini-competition.

Common pitfalls:

  • You assume membership means instant work. On a dynamic market, contracts are still competed. Budget your bidding time for that.
  • You miss the "reasonable period". The guidance says applications must be considered within a reasonable period, but it doesn't set a number of days. Apply well before you need to bid. That said, if you apply while a competition is running, the buyer must consider your application before excluding you.

How the Procurement Act 2023 changes framework entry for new suppliers

The Procurement Act 2023, in force since 24 February 2025, brought in open frameworks that must reopen on a set timetable, and dynamic markets that never close. Together they reduce the old problem of missing one tender and being locked out for four years.

The legal timetable for open frameworks is in section 49:

  • The first framework must be followed by a new award at least once within three years.
  • Each later framework must be followed by a new award at least once every five years.
  • The whole scheme must end within eight years of the first award.
  • If only one supplier is awarded, the term is capped at four years.

GOV.UK's frameworks guidance also confirms that suppliers can't join a closed framework part-way through. The only way in mid-life is when an open framework reopens.

For example, if an open framework is first awarded in May 2026, it has to reopen by May 2029 at the latest. If the buyer reopens it only once, that second framework can run to May 2034 at most. A supplier who misses the 2026 round has a guaranteed second chance within three years. The buyer can also reopen sooner, for example once a year.

Three practical points for SMEs:

  1. Reopening doesn't mean an easier test. You still submit a full tender. Read the earlier evaluation results if the buyer publishes them, so you know what scored well.
  2. Watch for the notice. Reopenings are advertised like a new procurement, so set up the same weekly Find a Tender search for frameworks you've missed.
  3. Fees are fixed for the life of the framework. Fees can only be charged to suppliers awarded a call-off, as a fixed percentage of estimated value (GOV.UK). If a buyer asks for an upfront fee to join, ask them what it's for.

The Act also changed how your capability is assessed, which matters as much as the timing. That's the next section.

What selection criteria and documents do you need to apply?

Buyers test your financial standing, technical ability and legal standing, and check exclusion grounds. Under the Act, any condition must be proportionate to the contract's nature, complexity and cost. Have your evidence pack ready before the notice appears.

Section 22 of the Act includes rules that help small suppliers:

  • A buyer can't ask for audited accounts unless you are, or were, legally required to have them audited under the Companies Act 2006. Many micro and small companies, sole traders and small charities aren't.
  • A buyer can't require contract insurance to be in place before the award. It can ask you to confirm you'll get it.
  • A buyer can't require you to have held previous contracts with a particular authority.
  • You can meet the conditions through associated suppliers, such as a consortium partner, or a subcontractor or guarantor with legally binding arrangements.

Here's a practical evidence pack to build once and reuse:

  1. Find a Tender share code, with Connected Persons and Exclusions filled in.
  2. Financial information: your last two years of accounts, or management accounts if you're newer, plus a short note explaining anything unusual.
  3. Insurance: current certificates, or a broker's letter confirming the cover levels you can get (for example, employer's liability and public liability limits).
  4. Three case studies of similar work: client type, scope, value, dates and results. Public sector experience isn't required.
  5. Referee contacts who have agreed to be contacted.
  6. Policies: health and safety, equality, data protection, safeguarding where relevant, and modern slavery if you meet the statutory threshold or the buyer asks for it.
  7. Social value evidence, because most frameworks score it. See Social Value in Tenders: PPN 002 Steps and Answer Examples.

The questionnaire layout varies by buyer. For a section-by-section walkthrough, read Selection Questionnaire Procurement Act 2023: 7 SME Steps.

Common mistakes and fixes:

  • A turnover test seems to rule you out. Check the lot value, not the total framework value. Then use the clarification facility to ask whether the condition is proportionate, or bid with a partner.
  • Your PSQ answers don't match your Find a Tender record. Buyers compare the two. Update your supplier information first, then make a new share code.

How mini-competitions and direct awards work once you're on a framework

A place on a framework doesn't guarantee any work. Most call-offs are run as mini-competitions among the framework suppliers. Some are direct awards, allowed only when the framework sets out an objective way to choose the supplier.

GOV.UK's guidance says that, unless there's only one supplier, a buyer can award without competition only when the framework sets out an objective mechanism. That might be a ranking from the framework tender, or the lowest price in a catalogue, together with the core terms.

A typical mini-competition goes like this:

  1. The buyer sends a call-off invitation to every supplier on the relevant lot, through the framework's portal.
  2. You get a specification, evaluation criteria (often a new quality and price split) and a deadline that's usually shorter than for an open tender.
  3. You submit a short response tailored to that buyer's problem.
  4. The buyer awards the contract and the framework fee applies only to that call-off value.

For example, imagine a training provider on a lot with eight suppliers. A council invites all eight to quote for a 20-day leadership programme, weighted 60% quality and 40% price. The provider's framework case studies help, but the deciding factor is its answer about this council's managers.

To turn membership into work:

  • Tell buyers you're on the framework. GCA has guidance on promoting your position as a supplier.
  • Answer every invitation. If you can't bid, decline formally rather than ignoring it. Some frameworks track how suppliers respond.
  • Keep your framework rates realistic. If direct awards go by price ranking, a high rate card means you won't be picked.

Common reasons SME bids get rejected at the framework stage

Bids are often rejected for administrative reasons, not because the quality is poor: missing exclusion declarations, weak technical evidence, incomplete pricing and late uploads. All of these can be fixed before you press submit.

The Act lists mandatory exclusion grounds in Schedule 6 and discretionary ones in Schedule 7. These cover you and your connected persons, which is why the Connected Persons section on Find a Tender matters.

Rejection causeWhat it looks likeFix
Exclusions section incompleteConnected persons left blank or a past issue not declaredComplete Connected Persons and Exclusions on Find a Tender. Explain any self-cleaning steps
Weak technical evidenceGeneric case studies, no figures, no datesMatch each case study to the lot specification. Give scope, value and results
Pricing schedule errorsBlank cells, altered formulas, wrong unitsFill in every cell. Don't change the template. Check the totals
Mandatory condition missedBidding for a lot outside your region or capacityBid only for lots you can deliver
Late or partial uploadPortal timed out at 11:58Submit at least 24 hours early. Download your submission receipt
Word limits exceededText cut off or marked downDraft offline, count words, then paste

For example, a social enterprise with a strong service could still fail the pass or fail stage because it left a director's details out of Connected Persons. Five minutes of admin would have stopped a month of bid writing from going to waste.

Ask for your feedback after every result. Under the Act, buyers have to give unsuccessful suppliers an assessment summary when they publish their award decision. Use that to plan your answers for the next reopening or a related framework.

Next steps

You can do the first two steps today without spending anything.

Do it yourself today:

  1. Create your GOV.UK One Login, choose Register an organisation on Find a Tender, and complete your supplier information up to Create a share code (official guide).
  2. Open GCA upcoming agreements and note any agreement or dynamic market in your sector, with its expected opening date.
  3. Start your evidence pack. Write your first two case studies using the format in the selection section above.

If you'd rather not do it all yourself:

  • Free official route: GCA and most councils run supplier engagement before a tender, and every live tender has a clarification facility. Both cost nothing. They suit you if you can write your own answers but need the rules clarified. They don't suit you if you have no time to write. The limitation is that buyers won't help you draft your bid.
  • Paid bid writing support: independent bid writers and tender consultancies can draft or review your PSQ and quality answers. Prices vary widely by scope and aren't published centrally, so get a fixed written quote and check what's included (as of October 2026; confirm with the provider). Paid support suits firms with a specific framework deadline and a decent chance of winning. It doesn't suit you if you can't meet the mandatory conditions yet, because no writer can fix that. A further limitation is that you still have to supply the evidence and pricing yourself.

Related guides on this site:

  • Selection Questionnaire Procurement Act 2023: 7 SME Steps
  • Social Value in Tenders: PPN 002 Steps and Answer Examples

FAQ

How long does it take to get on a framework agreement?

You can register on Find a Tender in an afternoon if your details are ready. The framework tender itself usually runs over several weeks, then evaluation, then award. With an open framework you might wait up to three years for a reopening if you miss the first round (s.49). Dynamic markets take applications at any time, but there's no fixed processing deadline.

Do you need a certain turnover to join a public sector framework?

There's no single legal minimum. Under section 22, any financial condition has to be proportionate to the contract's nature, complexity and cost. Buyers often compare your turnover with the lot or contract value, so check the condition for each lot you're interested in. If it rules you out, ask a clarification question or bid with a partner.

Can a sole trader or charity bid for a framework agreement?

Yes. Find a Tender accepts Charity Commission and other registration numbers, and it generates a unique identifier if you have none (GOV.UK). You can also tick that you're an SME or VCSE in your basic information. Buyers can't demand audited accounts you aren't legally required to have.

How much does it cost to apply for a government framework?

Registering on Find a Tender and viewing opportunities is free (GOV.UK). GCA charges no joining fee. Instead it takes a commission on the sales you make through the agreement, and the rate varies by agreement (GCA). Your real cost is the staff time spent writing bids.

What is the difference between a framework agreement and a direct contract?

A direct contract is for one specific piece of work with a fixed scope. A framework sets the terms and the list of suppliers, and buyers then award separate call-off contracts under it, by mini-competition or direct award. Being on a framework gives you no guaranteed income until you win a call-off.
